verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.
verse_text.line: Quiet, you're dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga.
verse_text.translation: Keep quiet and you are dumb; speak well and you are a babbler or a windbag; stay close and you are pushy; keep away and you lack confidence; be patient and you are a coward; refuse to put up with things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis.

reading: You feel passed over again and wonder if they are right about you. Bhartrihari says that when you serve a master, keeping quiet makes you dull, speaking well makes you a show-off, and being patient makes you weak. The verse points to a double bind where any behaviour gets read as a fault, not to a flaw in you. Today, this can name the structural bind you sit in at work, beyond your own standard to fix.
meaning: The poet Bhartrihari speaks to the reader from a section on wicked people. He describes the impossible position of anyone who serves a master. If you keep quiet, you are called dull. If you speak well, you are called a show-off. If you stay close, you are pushy. If you keep away, you lack confidence. If you are patient, you are weak. If you refuse to endure things, you are ill-bred. He says the duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis. You are wondering if they are right about you after being passed over again. The verse suggests the bind may sit in the structure of the role, not in your worth.

verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

reading: You feel unsure if you are leadership material while your manager gives visible projects to others. Manu tells Vishnu that even finding the wish-fulfilling tree, he hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, and doubt rises in his heart. This speaks to your unease today: the hesitation you feel may come from not knowing how generous the giver is, rather than from any lack in you. You might name what you truly want anyway, trusting that the one before you is ready to give.
meaning: Manu speaks to Vishnu after years of austerity. The Lord appears and offers any boon. Manu sees the divine feet and feels every wish fulfilled, yet one great longing remains. He compares himself to a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree but still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power. Doubt rises in his heart. The verse proposes that it is not too late to turn toward what matters, but it takes courage to ask for it. Your unease about the projects may come from not knowing how generous the one before you is, rather than from any lack in you.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna, seeing his own family in the enemy ranks, collapses in grief before the battle.
verse_text.line: Shaking limbs, a dry mouth, a racing body: the Gita opens with a panic attack, not a hero.
verse_text.translation: My limbs give way, my mouth is parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.

reading: You feel like you are good for nothing after your boss points out your mistakes in front of everyone. The Gita opens with Arjuna telling Krishna that his limbs give way, his mouth is parched, and his body trembles. When your work feels unsafe like this, your body can simply be reporting what is happening right now.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He has asked Krishna to drive the chariot between the two armies. He sees his teachers, uncles, sons and friends standing on the enemy side. His body reacts before his mind can catch up. His limbs give way, his mouth is parched, his body trembles and his hair stands on end. The verse reports what overwhelm does to a strong person. It proposes that a breakdown is a valid starting point, not a failure of character. Your body is reporting what your boss does to you in front of everyone. That shaking feeling is not proof that you are useless. It is simply what happens when work feels unsafe.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse_text.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

reading: Since the breakup, weekends have become just you. Ram tells Sita that speaking of pain lightens it a little, yet no one else can truly know this ache; only the heart alone knows the love it misses. You might find that naming this quiet solitude, even to yourself, carries a small weight away. Let the truth of what you miss rest in your own heart today.
meaning: Ram speaks to Sita while Hanuman carries the message across the sea. Sita sits captive and near despair in the grove. Hanuman has just dropped Ram's ring and told her Ram's story. Ram says that telling grief lightens it a little. Yet no one else can know this pain. Only his own heart knows the truth of the love between them. Since the breakup your weekends have become just you. Ram's words name the loneliness of a grief that no shared friend can fully hold.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You moved to a new city to start fresh after your divorce, knowing no one there. Lakshmana tells Ram that enthusiasm is powerful and there is no strength greater than it, so for the one who has it nothing is out of reach. In this unfamiliar place, a small act of will—reaching out to one person—can be the first step that makes the world feel reachable again.
meaning: At Lake Pampa, after Sita has been taken, Rama is overwhelmed by grief. Every bird and mated deer reminds him of her. Lakshmana pulls him out of despair. He tells Rama that enthusiasm is powerful and there is no strength greater than it. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach. The point is that beauty can sharpen grief, and a friend can remind you of your own strength. You moved to a new city to start fresh after your divorce, knowing no one there. A friend can remind you that a small act of will is enough to make the world feel reachable again.

verse_text.speaker: the gopis
verse_text.setting: The women of Braj, after Krishna has left, on missing him.
verse_text.line: "Since he left, it has been monsoon in our eyes."
verse_text.translation: Night and day our eyes keep raining. Ever since Shyam went away, it is always the rainy season for us.

reading: Since your closest friend moved abroad, it has been monsoon in your eyes. The gopis say night and day their eyes keep raining ever since Shyam went away, so that missing someone becomes a season rather than an event. You do not have to fix this weather; you can simply let it be what it is today.
meaning: The women of Braj speak these words after Krishna has gone. They tell a friend that since Shyam left their home, their eyes rain night and day. The verse says their weeping has become a season that never ends, not a single storm that passes. Your closest friend moving abroad has left a gap you only now see. The verse names that missing him can feel like weather that does not lift.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: You have been firefighting so long that there is nothing left in the tank. Bali, sitting by his window after ages of ruling, says again day, again night, the same chain of tasks; to a thinking person, this is a mockery. The verse names the loop you are in without calling it your fault. Let Bali’s words sit beside your empty tank today, simply as a mirror for the repetition you already feel.
meaning: The demon king Bali has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day he sits by his window and sees the same cycle of days and nights, the same duties rising and falling. He speaks to himself and says that to a thinking person this endless repetition feels like a mockery. The verse proposes that when life feels like a loop, the way forward is not more work but mastering the mind that runs it. Your firefighting has run the same loop so long that the tank feels dry. Bali names that exact loop without calling it your failure.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You feel the weight of work pressure that never eases, leaving you too tired to rise even on weekends. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go through contact with the senses, and they do not last. You can bear this fatigue without letting it sweep you into panic, trusting that this heavy stretch, too, will pass.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These feelings arrive and depart. They do not last. Arjuna must bear them patiently.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You lie awake with your mind spinning over whether the launch will work. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. Your thoughts tonight are not a sign you are failing at running your own thing; they are simply the wind moving. You can notice the spinning without forcing it to stop, and let your body rest beside it.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes the highest yogi who feels all beings' joy and pain as his own. Arjuna objects that such steady evenness cannot last, because the mind is too restless and strong. He says the mind is turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and as hard to hold as the wind. The Gita takes this complaint seriously and answers it. Your mind tonight is doing exactly what Arjuna named. The launch worries are not a sign you are failing at running your own thing; they are simply the wind moving.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse_text.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

reading: When colleagues carry MBAs and you hold only experience, you feel smaller beside them. Krishna tells Arjuna to raise himself by his own self and not let himself sink, because the self alone is the friend of the self. You do not have to push yourself down against their degrees; your own steadiness can be the ground that holds you up today.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the field of battle. Arjuna stands uncertain and burdened. Krishna tells him to be his own ally. He must lift himself by his own effort and not let himself sink. Depending on how he treats himself, Arjuna is either his own best friend or his own worst enemy. The choice lies in his own hands. Your experience is not less than their degrees. You can stop treating yourself as the one who falls short.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You lose your temper with your child over homework each evening and then hate yourself afterward. The Yoga Vasishtha describes a mind carried along on endless waves of tasks, caught in the loop of 'done this, doing this, must do that,' so that it never rests. When that loop tightens around you tonight, you might notice the mind fainting under its own reckonings, rather than judging the snap itself.
meaning: In the Yoga Vasishtha, two old friends meet again after years of hard austerity. Bhasa admits to Vilasa that he has never found peace. He explains that the mind is carried along on endless waves of tasks. It keeps reckoning, done this, doing this, must do that. Caught in that net of reckonings, the bird of the mind faints and never gets a moment's rest. The point is that years of effort without inner understanding leave a person exactly where they started. The same loop tightens around you when homework time begins. The verse shows that the snap is not the whole story. It is the mind fainting under its own endless reckonings.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You described a week where slamming doors and yelling leave you both feeling awful. The Yoga Vasishtha speaks of a mind caught in endless waves of 'done this, doing this, must do that,' where the bird of the mind faints in a net of reckonings. When the next slammed door echoes through your home, you might notice the background loop of tasks tightening, and simply let the mind rest in that understanding rather than adding another tally to the week.
meaning: Bhasa speaks to his old friend Vilasa, two men who grew up together in a forest hermitage and later spent years apart in hard austerities. When they meet again as old men, Vilasa asks if Bhasa has found peace. Bhasa answers that he has not, because the mind is carried along on endless waves of tasks. It never rests. It keeps reckoning: this I have done, this I am doing, this I must do. Caught in that net of reckonings, the bird of the mind faints. Your anger at the slammed door and the yelling comes from a mind that never stops tallying what is done and what is still owed. The verse names that loop rather than your failure in it.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.
verse_text.line: Quiet, you're dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga.
verse_text.translation: Keep quiet and you are dumb; speak well and you are a babbler or a windbag; stay close and you are pushy; keep away and you lack confidence; be patient and you are a coward; refuse to put up with things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis.

reading: You snapped after your lead dumped work on you and you became the problem. Bhartrihari writes that serving a master means any behaviour is read as a fault: quiet and you are dull, patient and you are weak. The bind is in the position, not in you. Today, your standup moment sits inside that same impossible structure.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks this from his section on the wicked. He is describing the courtier who serves a cruel master. The master turns every virtue into a fault. Stay silent and you are dull. Speak and you are a show-off. Be patient and you are weak. Refuse and you are ill bred. The duty of serving another is deeper than yoga. It means the bind belongs to the position, not to the person trying to serve. Your lead put his work on you and you snapped in standup. Now you carry the anger of being made the problem. The verse says the bind is in the position, not in you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: You are waiting for emergency leave while your dad is in hospice in Delhi. Krishna tells his mother Yashoda that since he left her, no one has called him by his pet name, and he has missed his morning breakfast and evening warm milk. In your distance, the ordinary tenderness you miss is real and mutual, not only yours. You might hold on to the simple fact that you are still called home, even across the miles.
meaning: Krishna sends a message through to his foster mother Yashoda. He is far from home in Mathura after killing. He tells her to stay well and that he and his brother will come in four or five days. He adds that since he left her, no one has called him Kanhaiya. He has not eaten morning breakfast or had warm milk in the evening. The verse proposes that missing home is love. It shows that the longing runs both ways. Krishna, now a prince, misses the ordinary tenderness of home. Your distance from your father does not make your missing him one-sided. The tenderness you feel is real, and it is felt across the miles too.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: The self was never born and never dies. It is not killed when the body is.
verse_text.translation: It is never born and never dies; having been, it will not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, constant and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.

reading: Watching your mother slowly go feels unbearable right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that the self was never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is slain. Let this truth sit quietly beside your grief today, as you hold her hand and witness her body fading.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is weeping because he must fight his own kin. Krishna tells him that the true self was never born and never dies. It remains eternal and ancient. When the body is slain, the self is not killed. Your mother's body is fading, but this teaching points to what outlasts that change. It does not erase what you are watching.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

meaning: Krishna sends a message through to his foster mother Yashoda. He is far away in Mathura after killing. He tells her to stay well and says his brothers and he will return in four or five days. He adds that since the day he left her, no one has called him by his pet name Kanhaiya. He has not eaten breakfast in the morning, nor he had warm milk in the evening. Your mother says she is fine, yet the distance between you still aches. This verse shows that missing home is itself a form of love, not a failure on your part.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: You spoke of anger leading to a harsh word about sending your father away, and now you cannot meet his eyes. Krishna tells his mother Yashoda that since leaving her, no one calls him by his pet name, and he has missed his morning breakfast and evening milk. This shows that even in separation, the ordinary tenderness of home is deeply missed. You might let this remind you of the simple name and care your father still holds for you.
meaning: Krishna sends a message to his foster-mother Yashoda through. He is far from in Mathura after killing. He tells her to stay well and that the brothers will come in four or five days. He adds that since the day he left her, no one has called him Kanhaiya. He has not eaten morning breakfast or had warm evening milk. The verse shows that missing home is love. It means that even a prince in separation longs for the ordinary tenderness of a pet name and a mother's food.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You yelled at your grandmother when she asked the same question for the fifth time, and she went quiet. Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against his will, as if pushed by force. That question can sit with you today: the moment you fear your own temper does not make you wicked, it marks a place where something inside pulled you forward, and noticing that pull is where understanding begins.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against his will, as if pushed by force. Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger. This anger clouds wisdom and acts like smoke over fire. The verse proposes that you see this pull clearly so you can master it. You fear your own temper because it moved faster than your care for her. Seeing that pull is the start of understanding, not proof that you are wicked.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You spoke unforgivable things to your business partner in a rage and lost the partnership, and the guilt stays. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born; from attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger. The verse speaks to you today by showing that the fire had been building before the words came. You can notice what your mind kept turning over before the snap, and let that awareness sit with the partnership you lost.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna has asked what a person of steady mind looks like in speech, posture and walk. Krishna answers by tracing a chain inward. When a person dwells on objects, attachment is born. From that attachment comes desire, and when that desire is blocked, it turns into anger. The verse proposes that steadiness is built by guarding where attention rests, because anger starts long before it flares. The anger that snapped at your partner did not appear from nowhere. It grew from something your mind kept turning over. That does not excuse the words, but it shows where the fire began.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Anger clouds judgement, clouded judgement loses memory, lost memory wrecks reason, and then you fall.
verse_text.translation: From anger comes delusion; from delusion, confusion of memory; from confusion of memory, the ruin of understanding; and with understanding ruined, a person is lost.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that from anger comes delusion, then confusion of memory, the ruin of understanding, and finally you fall. This is the Gita's view of how a surge can override the part of you that knew better, so the words come out before the storm passes. You can notice the shift when memory slips, and let that be the signal to pause before the next surge.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: It's desire, which turns into anger when blocked. Never satisfied, it is the real enemy here.
verse_text.translation: The Blessed Lord said: It is desire, it is anger, born of the quality of passion; all-devouring and greatly harmful. Know this to be the enemy here.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that desire, which becomes anger when blocked, is the real enemy here, never satisfied and all-devouring. You felt anger flare and then guilt stay after words you cannot take back. Notice the want behind the flash, not as your fault, but as the restless force Krishna names.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Unshaken in sorrow, not craving in joy, free of clinging, fear and anger: that is a steady mind.
verse_text.translation: One whose mind is not shaken by sorrow, who has no craving for pleasures, and who is free from attachment, fear and anger, is called a sage of steady mind.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that a steady mind is unshaken by sorrow, not craving in joy, and free of clinging, fear and anger. You still carry the guilt that stays after the anger flares, and this verse gives you ground to stand on: the steady person still feels everything, but sorrow, fear and anger no longer drive the response. Let that steadiness be your anchor today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Whoever can ride out the surge of desire and anger, here and now, is steady and happy.
verse_text.translation: One who is able, here in this life, before leaving the body, to withstand the surge born of desire and anger, is disciplined; he is a happy person.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever can withstand the surge of desire and anger here and now is steady and happy. The surge rises and falls on its own; your only task is to wait until it passes before you act. You could place your hand on your chest and simply notice the heat until it cools, without speaking or deciding anything.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on three kinds of food, effort, speech and giving.
verse_text.line: Speak words that don't wound, that are true, kind and helpful. That is discipline of speech.
verse_text.translation: Speech that causes no distress, that is truthful, pleasant and beneficial, and the regular study of sacred texts: this is called austerity of speech.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that disciplined speech means words that do not wound, that are true, kind and helpful. You could try letting that filter guide one conversation today, choosing words that carry your point without cruelty. This is how the surge passes into speech that rebuilds rather than breaks.

story.title: Vishvamitra's vow
story.summary: Vishvamitra had given up a kingdom to become a sage, and had already started his effort over more than once. Then, tested again, he lost his temper and cursed the apsara Rambha, and with that curse the power of his long austerity was spent. This time he made a vow: he would not give way to anger, or even speak. He kept a long silence. Obstacles came again and shook him, but anger couldn't get in. In the end he reached his goal, and Vasishtha, the rival he had once fought, embraced him as a friend.
story.lesson: Relapses happen. A clear vow and steady practice can loosen anger's grip.

days.reading: Vishvamitra, after losing his temper and wasting years of austerity, vowed never again to yield to anger or even speak. He kept a long silence, faced fresh obstacles, and let that steady practice carry him to his goal, where his old rival embraced him. Your guilt stayed after the rage passed; this shows that a clear vow and quiet practice can loosen anger’s grip without erasing what already happened.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You feel dropped out and without direction, with nothing seeming worth the effort anymore. Young Rama asks what a kingdom or pleasure is to him, who he is, and what all this is for. This verse meets your emptiness as a real question rather than a failure, opening the space to ask who you are beneath the drift.
meaning: Young Rama has come back from his travels and sits in his father's court. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask why he looks so low. Rama answers that nothing interests him anymore. He asks what kingship or pleasure mean to him. He asks who he really is and what all this is for. He says if the world is unreal, let it be unreal. He asks whose it is and what anyone has gained. The text treats this honest naming of emptiness as the first step of inquiry, not as the final answer. Your dropped out feeling and your sense that nothing is worth the effort is met here as a real question, not a personal failure. It opens space to look beneath the drift instead of fixing it right away.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

meaning: Young Rama stands in his father's court after returning from travel. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask why he has gone so quiet and lost in himself. Rama answers that the crown and every pleasure feel hollow to him. He asks who he really is and what all this striving is for. He suggests that if the world is unreal, then let it be unreal, and asks whose it truly is and what anyone has actually gained. The text treats this honest naming of emptiness as the first healthy step toward real inquiry.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: You have spent fifteen years in twelve-hour days building this business, and now the work leaves you feeling empty and tired. Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and says again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks, and to a thinking person this feels like a mockery. Your own repetition might be speaking to you that same way today, naming the exhaustion without judging the years you gave.
meaning: King Bali, who has ruled the three worlds for ages, sits by his window and watches the same days pass. He speaks to himself about the endless round of waking and sleeping, eating and ruling. He says the same chain of tasks returns again and again. To a thinking person, this repetition feels like a mockery. After fifteen years of long days you built this business, and now the work leaves you empty and tired. The verse names that same loop without asking you to leave it behind.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Rama describes his restless mind to the sages.
verse_text.line: The mind pounces on a task like a bird on food, then drops it like a bored child's toy.
verse_text.translation: The mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy.

reading: You plan to study after work, yet end up scrolling until 1am. Rama tells the sages that the mind swoops onto a task like a bird onto meat, then drops it like a bored child's toy. This restless pattern is simply how the untrained mind behaves, not a mark against you. Tonight, when you close the screen, notice the mind's quick swoop and let it land without blame.
meaning: Rama speaks to the sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha after they ask why he has grown so withdrawn. He has seen wealth harden people, time eat everything, and ego and craving drive us. He laments that the mind never fills. In this moment he names the restless habit: it grabs at whatever attracts it and then abandons it, almost at once. He offers no solution here. He only points out the pattern honestly. Your evening plan to study and your actual scrolling are part of the same restless habit, not proof that you lack will. Naming it is already a step forward.

verse_text.speaker: Savitri
verse_text.setting: Knowing her husband will die in three days, Savitri takes a hard three-night vow; her father-in-law worries.
verse_text.line: I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end.
verse_text.translation: Don't be distressed, father. I will see this vow through. It was begun with determination, and determination is what carries it to the end.

reading: You have a firm resolve for your GATE preparation, yet starting each day consumes half your time. Savitri tells her worried father-in-law that she began this vow with determination, and that same determination will carry it to the end. Let that steady resolve be the force that carries you from the moment you sit down to study today.
meaning: Savitri speaks to her blind father-in-law, the exiled king Dyumatsena. She knows her husband Satyavan will die in three days. She has begun a severe three-night vow without food. Dyumatsena is distressed by the harshness. Savitri tells him she started with firm resolve, and that same resolve will carry the vow to its end. You have set your mind on the GATE exam. The daily start still swallows half your morning. Savitri's words point to the same force that began your plan. Let it carry you from the chair to the page.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: Your business has reached its best year ever, and you feel thankful while wanting to keep your feet on the ground. Bhartrihari says he does not know what generous austerity ripened into this freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, good company, learning that brings calm, and a mind that stirs only gently. You can meet this gratitude today by quietly noticing the ordinary dignities you already hold—your own hours, honest work, and a quiet mind—and simply resting in them.
meaning: The poet Bhartrihari speaks these lines from his Worship of Shiva. He is reflecting on the life of a wanderer who has left behind palaces. He lists the gifts he now holds. He names freedom to move as he wishes, food that he eats without shame, company with noble people, learning that ends only in calm, and a mind that stays gentle even when it looks at the world. He wonders aloud what generous austerity could have produced such a life. He treats these plain goods as a rare blessing, not something earned or ordinary.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You feel that everything is good, with peace and gratitude in your heart. The poet wonders at a plain, self-respecting life—freedom to move, food eaten without humiliation, good company, and a mind that stirs only gently. This quiet ease you carry today is the very calm such a life names, and it is worth simply resting in.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines from his Worship of Shiva. He is a poet who has left behind palace life for a quiet existence by the Ganga. He looks at his simple daily goods and wonders at them. He lists freedom to wander, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, and a mind that stirs only gently even after long outward looking. He says he does not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of. You feel that everything is good, with peace and gratitude in your heart. This quiet ease you carry today is the very calm such a life names, and it is worth simply resting in.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people worship him: those in distress, those seeking knowledge, those seeking wealth, and the wise. You felt drawn to Krishna while starting the Gita, and this verse names curiosity as one of those open doors. You do not have to arrive with perfect understanding; your quiet pull is already counted among what Krishna welcomes.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, those who seek knowledge, those who seek wealth, and the wise. He says all four worship him. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. Your quiet pull toward Krishna while raising your children is one of those open doors. You do not need to arrive with perfect understanding.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Your meditation and chanting have brought you calm, and now you wish to go deeper toward God. Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people worship him: those in distress, those curious, those in need, and the wise. Your path from calm practice into deeper devotion is one of those welcomed doors, and you can rest in that as you sit today.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after noting that the deluded do not turn to him. He names four kinds of good people who do worship him. These are the distressed, the curious, those in need, and the wise. He says all four are welcome. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is accepted. It does not demand a pure motive or a single reason. Your calm from meditation and chanting is already a valid starting point. The wish to go deeper toward God enters through one of these four doors, and that door is open to you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You wish to carry the joy of singing bhajans into every moment. Krishna tells Arjuna that people turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom, and he calls all four kinds of seekers good. If your heart longs for that same delight beyond the singing, you may rest in the truth that coming with a simple desire is already welcomed.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, the curious, those in need, and the wise. He calls all four worshippers welcome. The verse says that whatever brings a person to the search is accepted. You carry a wish to let the delight of your bhajans fill every hour. The verse holds that a simple longing is already a worthy way in.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse_text.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

reading: You are launching your product next month, and the thought of it failing weighs on you. Krishna tells Arjuna that your right is only to the work itself, never to its fruits, and that this should not make you stop. You can keep preparing and showing up for what is in your hands, while letting the result rest where it will.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna stands between two armies, unsure whether to fight. Krishna tells him that a person has a right only to the action itself, never to the fruits that follow. The teaching is to do the work fully, yet let go of owning the outcome. Inaction is not the answer either. You are building something of your own, and the money behind it feels fragile. The verse asks you to keep your hands on the work you can control, and let the launch outcome rest on its own.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You are carrying the work of colleagues who were let go, waiting to see if you are next. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go, and do not last; bear them. This week’s heavier load is one of those passing contacts, not a permanent state. When the next update arrives, let the waiting itself be something that comes and goes.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These experiences arrive and depart on their own. They do not last. Therefore Arjuna must bear them with patience. The teaching rests on the idea that the true self outlasts every bodily change and every passing feeling. The heavier load and the waiting are contacts that come and go. They do not define the part of you that remains when the workday ends.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they are spoken. In the Shanti Parva, Krishna says his heart is churned like a fire-stick, and the harsh words his relatives say keep burning him day after day. You are feeling that same sting today, pushed out because you could not give them a son. The verse names the burn without asking you to carry it forever.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after growing weary of feuds within his own clan. He tells Narada that he gives his kin half of what he possesses and bears their harsh words, yet those words still grind his heart like a fire-stick being churned for flame. The verse proposes that in family conflicts, the only effective weapon is not force but gentleness, patience and respect. Your husband's family pushed him to leave you because you could not give them a son. The verse names that burn without asking you to carry it forever.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: The self was never born and never dies. It is not killed when the body is.
verse_text.translation: It is never born and never dies; having been, it will not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, constant and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.

reading: You carry the hurt of missing your father’s final rites. Krishna tells Arjuna that the self was never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is slain. Let this thought sit beside your grief today, as you hold the memory of who he was beyond the body he left behind.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is shaken by the prospect of fighting his own kin. Krishna tells him that the self inside every person was never born and never dies. It does not end when the body is destroyed. The self is eternal, constant and ancient. It simply outlasts the changes that bodies go through. Your father is gone from his body, but the self that lived in him was never born and will not cease. That thought can sit beside the ache of missing his final rites.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: As we drop worn-out clothes and put on new ones, the self leaves a worn body for a new one.
verse_text.translation: Just as a person casts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied self casts off worn-out bodies and enters others that are new.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the self casts off worn-out clothes and enters new ones, just as a person changes garments. This picture of setting aside a worn body can offer you a gentle image of transition, since your own tradition holds rebirth. Let this idea of laying down an old garment stand as solid ground beneath you today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Childhood, youth, old age: the body keeps changing. The wise aren't thrown by the next change.
verse_text.translation: Just as the embodied self passes through childhood, youth and old age in this body, so it passes on to another body. The steady person is not bewildered by this.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the embodied self simply passes through childhood, youth, and old age, and then moves on to another body. You have already watched someone you love change across those stages, and now you are facing the hardest shift of all. The verse invites you to notice the continuity that remains even as the form changes, giving you something solid to stand on today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: No weapon cuts it, no fire burns it, no water wets it, no wind dries it.
verse_text.translation: Weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it, water does not wet it, and wind does not dry it.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that no weapon cuts the self, no fire burns it, no water wets it, and no wind dries it. Whatever reached the body at the end, through illness or age, did not touch who they were. You can stand on this image quietly today: the part of your dad that mattered was beyond the reach of what happened.

verse_text.speaker: Vasishtha
verse_text.setting: Vasishtha on the fourth gatekeeper: good company (satsanga).
verse_text.line: Even at your lowest and most helpless, don't let go of good company.
verse_text.translation: Even when people fall into the hardest straits and feel helpless, they should not let go of good company, not even a little.

days.reading: Vasishtha tells Rama that even when people fall into the hardest straits and feel helpless, they should not let go of good company, not even a little. This speaks to the isolation that can follow a loss like your father's, when the world keeps moving and you feel alone in your hurt. Let one steady thread remain—a brief word with someone who steadies you, even for a few minutes.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on simple, wholehearted devotion.
verse_text.line: A leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water: whatever is offered with love, I accept.
verse_text.translation: Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, that offering of love from the pure-hearted I accept.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that he accepts a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or a little water when offered with love. You could place a flower or a small glass of water near your dad’s photo today, letting your love have a simple place to rest. The verse says the offering is received because of the heart behind it, not its size.

story.title: Bharata returns to Ayodhya
story.summary: Bharata was far away at his grandfather's home when his father, King Dasharatha, died. Messengers called him back without telling him why. He rode into an Ayodhya that had gone quiet, went looking for his father, and learned he was gone. He fell to the ground and wept. When he could stand again, the family priest Vasishtha gently told him it was time to perform the last rites, and he did them, grieving as he went.
story.lesson: Missing the goodbye is its own grief. Let yourself feel it, then do what love asks next.

days.reading: Valmiki’s Ramayana tells of Bharata returning to Ayodhya to find his father dead, then grieving as he performs the last rites. Missing the goodbye is its own grief, and your pain over not reaching the cremation is real. Let that sorrow sit with you, then do what love asks next in the quiet moments with your children.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You are stretched across office deadlines, your son's exam prep, and a toddler. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go, and do not last; you are asked to bear them patiently. This restlessness can be met as weather that shifts, not a permanent state to fight. When the next deadline or exam prep arrives, notice that it, too, is a contact that will pass.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that the true self is never born and never dies. Yet the body still meets cold and heat, pleasure and pain through the senses. These feelings come and go. They do not last. Arjuna must learn to bear them patiently without being carried away by either joy or grief. Your restlessness is a contact between your senses and the demands on you. It has a beginning and it will have an end. You do not have to fight it as if it is the whole of you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: With work ramping up, daycare calling about fevers, and your partner away, you are caught in contacts that touch and move on. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go; they do not last, so bear them. Today, this means the fever call and the deadline are weather passing through, not a permanent state you carry alone.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These sensations come and they go. They do not last. So Arjuna must bear them with patience. The teaching rests on the idea that the self within outlasts every bodily change and every passing feeling. Your body and your day are meeting hard things right now, and those meetings pass even when they feel endless.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You are starting your dream job on Monday, and excitement sits beside terror. Lakshmana tells Ram that there is no strength greater than enthusiasm, and for the one who has it, nothing is out of reach. Your energy right now can meet this new chapter without erasing the fear.
meaning: At Lake Pampa, after Sita has been taken, Rama is surrounded by the beauty of spring and sinks deeper into grief. Lakshman, Rama's younger brother, pulls him from despair. He tells him that enthusiasm is powerful and there is no strength greater than it. For the person who has this energy, nothing in the world is out of reach. The verse proposes that resolute will is the strongest resource a person has, and with it little in the world lies beyond reach. Your excitement for Monday already holds real force. The terror does not cancel it out. That mix is simply the ground you stand on as you begin.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You have been going back and forth on leaving your job for months, and it occupies your thoughts day and night. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. Today, your looping thoughts about this decision mirror that same restlessness, yet the verse names it as a force outside your command rather than a flaw in you.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He has just heard that a steady person treats joy and pain as the same. Arjuna objects. He says his mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He thinks it is as hard to hold as the wind. The verse proposes that this restlessness is real, but practice and letting go can train the mind over time. Your looping thoughts about the job are not a sign that you are failing at this decision. They are the mind doing what Arjuna named, restless and hard to steady.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You are moving from one thing to the next, and the tiredness stays even on holidays. The Yoga Vasishtha has Bhasa say that a mind caught on waves of endless tasks—'done this, doing this, must do that'—faints in worry and never rests. Your fraying may be the mind's net of reckonings tightening, not a lack in you. Notice one small task today and let your mind step back from the list just for that moment.
meaning: Bhasa speaks to Vilasa after they meet again as old men. Vilasa asks if he has found peace. Bhasa answers that he has not. He says the mind is carried on great waves of tasks. It never rests. It dances with worry. It reckons, done this, doing this, must do that. Caught in that net, the bird of the mind faints. The verse proposes that years of hard effort without inner understanding leave a person exactly where they started. Your tiredness staying through holidays fits what Bhasa describes. The fraying comes from the mind's endless list, not from a lack in you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse_text.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

reading: Karmaṇy evādhikāras te: your right is to the action. Fear of failure is a fear about the fruit, which was never given to you to control. Krishna also closes the escape route: don't let this make you stop acting. Care, prepare and aim well, then put the outcome down.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is afraid to fight his own teachers and relatives. Krishna tells him that his duty is to act with full attention. He must not cling to what will come after. The results belong to a larger order, not to Arjuna alone. Krishna insists that this does not mean Arjuna should do nothing. Your presentation belongs to your effort alone. The laughter you imagine belongs to a result you were never meant to control.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

reading: You are caught between two costly paths and do not know which is right. Arjuna tells Krishna that his mind is confused about what is right, and he asks plainly to be taught what is best. In your present moment, you can lay this uncertainty before what you trust, asking for clarity without forcing the choice yourself. Let your honest admission of not knowing open the way forward.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

reading: You are caught between bringing your mother to you or returning to Patna alone. Arjuna tells Krishna his mind is confused about what is right and asks plainly to be taught what is best. Saying you do not yet know the way forward can itself be the first step toward seeing it. When you sit with your mother in Patna, let that honest uncertainty sit beside you.
meaning: Arjuna stands on the battlefield and tells Krishna that his mind is clouded by weakness. He says he cannot tell which choice is right. He asks Krishna to teach him plainly what is best. He offers himself as a student who has come to learn. You are facing two heavy paths and your own judgment feels unreliable right now. Admitting that you do not yet know the way forward is not a failure. It is the honest ground from which a clearer choice can grow.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that it is better to walk one's own path, even imperfectly, than to perform another's duty flawlessly. When your batchmate's promotion stirs a hard knot in you, this points to the weight of measuring your step against his. Your own work still belongs to you, and living from it carries its own quiet worth.
meaning: Krishna speaks this to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just explained that a person reaches perfection by doing their own work as worship. Now he repeats that one's own duty, even if done imperfectly, is better than another's duty performed flawlessly. He adds that acting in line with one's own nature brings no fault. Your batchmate's promotion sits in your chest like a stone. The verse asks you to feel the weight of that comparison without letting it rewrite what your own work means to you.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You keep buying things and upgrading, yet nothing fills the space. Young Rama asks the sages in his father's court what kingship or pleasure mean to him, and who he really is. That same question can sit with you today: the emptiness after the upgrade is not a failure, but the opening of a real inquiry into what actually matters.
meaning: Young Rama has returned from his travels and sits in his father's court. The sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask him why he seems so low. Rama answers that he no longer finds interest in anything around him. He asks what kingship or pleasure mean to him, and who he really is. He wonders what all this is for, and whether it is unreal. If it is unreal, let it be unreal. He asks whose it is and what anyone has gained. The verse names this honest emptiness as the first step of inquiry. Your cycle of upgrades leaves the same hollow space because the chase itself has lost its shape. Rama names that void as a real starting point, not a flaw to fix.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You have sent out many applications since your company shut down, and now nothing has come back. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in his chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. In the same way, your stopping right now is simply the moment when grief has taken away the will to act. The story does not end there: the next verses turn toward asking for help and finding a way forward.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. Arjuna has just argued that killing his own kin would destroy their families and ways of life. He says he would rather be killed unarmed. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna drops his bow and arrows and sits down on the chariot seat. His mind is overwhelmed by grief. The verse names a breakdown. It shows that even the strongest person can freeze when grief takes over the will to act.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You come home to an empty apartment, eat, sleep, and repeat, with no one to share it and no sure sense of what any of it is for. Young Rama asks, what is a kingdom or pleasure to me, who am I, and what is all this for? This same questioning of everything he has built can sit with you today as an honest opening, not a flaw to fix.
meaning: Young Rama has returned from his travels and sits in his father's court. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask him why he looks so low. Rama answers that nothing interests him. He asks what kingship or pleasure mean to him, who he really is, and what all this is for. He says if it is unreal, let it be unreal, and asks whose it is and what anyone has gained. The text treats this questioning as the honest start of inquiry, not as a final answer. Your routine of coming home, eating, and sleeping carries the same honest weight. Rama's question names what you feel without rushing to fix it.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.
verse_text.line: Quiet, you're dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga.
verse_text.translation: Keep quiet and you are dumb; speak well and you are a babbler or a windbag; stay close and you are pushy; keep away and you lack confidence; be patient and you are a coward; refuse to put up with things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis.

reading: You trained your nephew, yet any move you make now seems to be read as a fault. Bhartrihari writes that serving a powerful master is a double bind: stay quiet and you are dull, speak up and you are a show-off. This verse names that impossible position, not your own failing. Today, you might anchor in your own standard of work rather than hunting for one right behaviour that will finally be accepted.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks this from the section on the wicked. He is describing the courtier who serves a cruel master. The master turns every trait into a fault. Stay silent and you are dull. Speak well and you are a windbag. Stay close and you are pushy. Keep away and you lack confidence. Be patient and you are weak. Refuse to endure and you are ill bred. Serving another is a duty so deep that even yogis cannot master it. Your nephew took your clients after you trained him. Now any move you make feels read as a fault. The verse names that double bind, not your own failing.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You described your hands shaking after a road-rage outburst at a signal. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born, then desire, and then anger. Your flare-up may trace back to something you kept turning over before the horn blared. Notice the moment your mind begins dwelling, and let that awareness sit with you the next time you grip the wheel.
meaning: Krishna answers Arjuna's question about what a steady person looks like. Arjuna wants to know how someone of settled wisdom speaks, sits and walks. Krishna explains that when a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger. Your hands shook after the outburst at the signal. The flare may trace back to something you kept turning over before the horn blared.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna

verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.

reading: You get irritated so fast these days. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born, and from attachment comes desire, then anger. The verse points to the moment before the snap, where keeping something in mind turns into a wanting that hardens. You might notice the irritation building in the pause before you speak.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after Arjuna asks how a person of steady wisdom speaks, sits and walks. Krishna traces the inner sequence. When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger. The verse proposes that steadiness is built by guarding attention, because anger starts with what a person keeps dwelling on. Your irritation flares fast because something has been sitting in your mind long enough to become a need. The verse points to that buildup, not the final snap.

reading: You feel angry because a small mistake by your staff ruined your whole day. Notice what object your thoughts were dwelling on, and see if the anger loosens when that dwelling stops.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after Arjuna asks how a person of steady wisdom sits, speaks and walks. Krishna traces the inner movement that unsettles even a wise person. He says that when someone dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire, and from desire comes anger. The verse proposes that steadiness is built by guarding where attention rests, because anger begins with what a person keeps turning over in the mind. Your flare up after a small staff mistake may trace back to something you kept turning over before the day began.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: Your temper spikes when your partner breaks an agreement, and then you lie awake replaying how loud you got. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, as hard to hold as the wind. That same stormy quality is what keeps you awake tonight, turning the evening into a loop you cannot switch off.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes the highest yogi who feels all beings' joy and pain as his own. Arjuna objects that such evenness cannot last. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. It is as hard to hold as the wind. The Gita takes this complaint seriously and answers that practice and letting go can train it. The same restlessness that flares when your partner breaks an agreement is now replaying the scene at night, and the verse names that storm without asking you to stop it.

Your phone hitting the wall is the visible burst; the dwelling that fed it happened earlier, in the space between the irritation and the throw.

When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire. From desire comes anger. The verse shows that anger does not appear from nowhere. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born, and from attachment comes desire, and from desire comes anger. In that traffic, the slowdown meets a wanting you had been turning over, and the anger rises. The wheel under your hands is real, and the heat in your chest is real too.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna has just asked what a person of steady wisdom looks like in speech, posture and walk. From that attachment comes desire, and when desire meets a block, anger arises. The verse shows the chain, not your fault for being in the car.

Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born, and from attachment comes desire, then anger. That same fire can begin earlier, in the moment you keep turning the changed brief over in your mind and it begins to feel like something you need. From that attachment comes desire, and when desire is blocked, it turns into anger. The verse traces how a mind that keeps returning to the same thing can move from quiet focus to wanting, and then to rage.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You said something nasty to your best friend in a fight about nothing, and now it is awkward. Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does the wrong thing even against his will, as if pushed by force. The verse names that inner push without calling you wicked for it. Today, you might notice the moment your anger takes over before the words come out, and simply hold that awareness with your friend.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even when he does not want to, as if pushed by some force. Krishna answers that unfulfilled desire turns into anger, and this anger is the enemy that clouds a person's wisdom like smoke over fire. The verse proposes that a person can master this force by seeing it clearly for what it is. Your anger took the wheel in a fight that meant nothing, and now the space between you and your best friend feels heavy. The verse names that inner push without calling you wicked for it.

The flare-up you feel may be the final spark of something you kept turning over earlier. Notice the moment before the snap, when the mind is still resting on the trigger.
meaning: Krishna answers Arjuna, who has asked what a person of steady mind looks like. Krishna explains that when someone dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire, and when that desire is blocked, it turns into anger. The verse traces how attention fixed on things leads step by step to wrath and ruin. Your flare at the office may be the last link in a chain you started earlier, when your mind kept returning to the same slight.

reading: Krishna starts earlier than the outburst. Dhyāyato viṣayān puṃsaḥ: when you keep dwelling on something, you get attached, attachment turns into wanting, and wanting that meets a wall turns into anger. By the time you snap, the fire has been building for a while.

Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born, and from attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger. Today, this points to the moment before the flare, when your mind keeps turning over the wait or the service. You might notice the heat building while you are still waiting, rather than only after the words come out.
meaning: Krishna is answering Arjuna, who has asked what a person of steady mind looks like in speech, posture and walk. Krishna traces how the mind moves. Your irritation with delivery people and waiters may begin earlier than the moment you snap, in the quiet turning over of what you want to happen.
