From that attachment comes desire. When desire meets an obstacle, it turns into anger. The verse proposes that steadiness begins with guarding where attention rests, because anger does not appear without this prior dwelling. Your anger has its own early stage, before the snap. This verse traces how dwelling on something hard can harden into wanting and then into rage.

verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You are watching peers raise funding while you still work alone from your spare room. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sank onto his chariot seat, his mind overwhelmed by grief. In your own moment of feeling stuck, this verse names the weight of sitting down when the road ahead looks long. The greatest archer of his time simply stopped, and the story still moved forward from there.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. He reports that Arjuna has just laid down his bow and arrows and sat down in his chariot. His mind is overwhelmed by grief. The verse marks the lowest point of the opening chapter. Even the greatest warrior freezes when the cost of action feels too high. The teaching begins from this breakdown rather than from strength.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': the poet to his own hope.
verse_text.line: I swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. Hope, how much longer will you make me dance?
verse_text.translation: I somehow put up with the taunts of the wicked while trying to please them; I held back my tears and laughed with an empty heart; I folded my hands even before people whose minds were numbed by money. Hope, futile hope, how much more will you make me dance?

reading: Seeing your juniors reach the top stings. Bhartrihari cries out to hope, saying he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart, dancing only because hope kept pulling him. You do not have to keep performing for an update that keeps hurting you; you can notice what you are swallowing today and let your own heart stop dancing to their rhythm.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines to his own hope during a confession of craving. He tells hope that he endured the taunts of wicked people, held back his tears, and forced laughter with an empty heart. He also folded his hands before those numbed by money. He asks how much longer hope will make him dance in this futile way. You are watching people you once worked beside rise to the top, and each update cuts you. The verse names the cost of swallowing that sting to keep hoping for your own recognition.

meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. Arjuna has just argued that killing his kin would destroy families and ways of life. He says he would rather be killed unarmed. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna sinks down on the chariot seat, letting his bow and arrows fall, his mind overwhelmed by grief. Arjuna froze because the cost became too visible. Your freeze comes from watching others move while you are still at the starting line.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that doing one's own duty, even imperfectly, is better than performing another's duty perfectly. When you measure your home and career against the other mums, you are weighing your own path against theirs. Your choice to raise your children is your own duty walked honestly, and it carries no wrong simply because it looks different from theirs.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield after listing duties tied to different ways of life. Arjuna is caught between grief and action. Krishna tells him that one reaches perfection by doing the work that fits one's own nature. He says that one's own path, even if walked imperfectly, is better than another's done perfectly. Acting in line with one's own nature brings no fault. Your choice to raise your children is your own path walked honestly. It carries no wrong simply because it looks different from the careers and homes the other mums display.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse_text.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

reading: At every family dinner, you feel like the other one beside your sister’s shine. Krishna tells Arjuna to raise himself by his own self and not let himself sink, because the self alone is the friend of the self. You can choose to be the friend who lifts you up at that table, steady in your own worth.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on acting free of ego, like and dislike, in your own way.
verse_text.line: Better your own path done imperfectly than someone else's done perfectly. Borrowed lives are dangerous.
verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, even done imperfectly, than the duty of another well done. Better is death in one's own duty; the duty of another is full of fear.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that doing your own path imperfectly is better than doing someone else's perfectly, and that borrowing another's life brings fear. When family dinners highlight your sister's achievements, this verse sees the danger in measuring your worth against her route. It invites you to notice your own duty as yours, not as a grade against hers.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how the wise live and work.
verse_text.line: Content with what comes, beyond envy, steady in success and failure, you stay free even while working.
verse_text.translation: Content with whatever comes unasked, beyond the pairs of opposites, free from envy, the same in success and failure, even when acting he is not bound.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the wise stay content with what arrives unasked, free from envy and steady in success and failure, remaining unbound even while acting. You do not have to measure yourself against your sister's path or the other seat at family dinners. Let your own work be enough for today, without glancing sideways at hers.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Drop the cravings, the sense of 'mine' and the 'I' that keeps score. That's where peace is.
verse_text.translation: The person who gives up all desires and moves about free from longing, without the sense of 'mine' and without ego, attains peace.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to drop the cravings, the sense of 'mine', and the 'I' that keeps score, saying that is where peace is. You carry the weight of being the other one at every family dinner. Let go of the scorekeeper that ranks you against her path, and rest in the peace of moving through your own studies without that tally.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna it is better to walk one's own path, even imperfectly, than to perform another's duty perfectly. At every family dinner, the spotlight falls on your sister's achievements, yet your own studies have their own shape. You could spend today listing one task that belongs only to your course, not hers.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Doing your own work well can be your worship of the source of all life.
verse_text.translation: By worshipping, through his own work, Him from whom all beings arise and by whom all this is pervaded, a person attains perfection.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that doing your own work well, as an offering to the source of all life, brings perfection. You could treat one small study task today as your own offering, without measuring it against your sister's path. Your effort belongs to you, and it stands complete on its own.

story.title: The mongoose and the handful of flour
story.summary: At the end of Yudhishthira's grand horse sacrifice, a mongoose appeared with one side of its body made of gold. It declared that the whole sacrifice was worth less than a handful of flour. Once, it said, during a famine, a poor gleaner and his family each gave their last share of flour to a hungry guest. When the mongoose rolled in the flour that had spilled, half its body turned gold. It had gone to many great sacrifices since, hoping to turn the other half, and none had done it.
story.lesson: A small gift, honestly earned and given from little, outweighs the grandest show.

days.reading: A mongoose tells Yudhishthira that his grand sacrifice was worth less than a poor family’s last handful of flour, because they gave it honestly from scarcity. This speaks to your hurt at always being the other one at family dinners, showing that a small, real offering carries more weight than any grand display. Let your own steady path be that handful of flour.

reading: Your brother's shop runs twice as well, and relatives count it at every wedding. Krishna says it is better to walk your own path, even imperfectly, than to perform another's duty perfectly. You do not have to match his scale to carry worth in your own work today.

Krishna says one's own duty, even if done imperfectly, is better than another's duty performed perfectly. Acting in line with one's own nature brings no fault. Your worth does not sit on the scale of your brother's shop. The verse asks you to see your own work as enough, flaws and all.

reading: You moved for a better life and find yourself measuring it against friends who stayed in India. Krishna tells Arjuna that it is better to walk one's own duty, even imperfectly, than to perform another's path well. Your own path can hold its own worth today, without needing to match how comfortably others live nearby.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna stands between two armies and feels the weight of what he must do. Krishna tells him that each person has duties that fit their own nature. It is better to walk your own path, even if you stumble along it, than to perform someone else's path with perfect skill. Doing the work that matches who you are does not bring fault upon you. You left India to build a life on your own terms. That choice already carries its own dignity, even when the days feel heavier than the ones your friends know.

verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

reading: Comparison is mostly a voice that pushes you down. Krishna says you can be your own friend or your own enemy, and asks you to lift yourself up. Start by noticing which one you've been lately.
meaning: Krishna speaks this to Arjuna while they talk about staying steady when honour and insult come. Arjuna has been asking how to keep balance when the world judges him. Krishna tells him to be his own friend. The self alone can lift the self up, and the self alone can drag the self down. It is a choice about how you treat your own mind. When comparison makes you feel small, this points to the voice inside that either builds you up or weighs you down. It asks you to notice which side you have been on lately.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on acting free of ego, like and dislike, in your own way.
verse_text.line: Better your own path done imperfectly than someone else's done perfectly. Borrowed lives are dangerous.
verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, even done imperfectly, than the duty of another well done. Better is death in one's own duty; the duty of another is full of fear.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna it is better to follow your own path, even imperfectly, than to do another’s perfectly. Borrowing someone else’s life brings fear, because comparison quietly swaps your way for theirs and then grades you on a foreign scale. You can notice when your peace slips because you are measuring yourself against a borrowed standard, and return to the one path that is actually yours.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how the wise live and work.
verse_text.line: Content with what comes, beyond envy, steady in success and failure, you stay free even while working.
verse_text.translation: Content with whatever comes unasked, beyond the pairs of opposites, free from envy, the same in success and failure, even when acting he is not bound.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the wise are content with what comes unasked, free from envy, and steady through success and failure even while working. This speaks to the restlessness that comparison brings, offering ground to stand on in your own lane. You can keep your ambition while letting go of the sideways glance at others' gains.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Drop the cravings, the sense of 'mine' and the 'I' that keeps score. That's where peace is.
verse_text.translation: The person who gives up all desires and moves about free from longing, without the sense of 'mine' and without ego, attains peace.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to drop the cravings, the sense of 'mine,' and the 'I' that keeps score, because that is where peace is. When comparison runs all day, it is this scorekeeper measuring you against others. You can loosen that measuring stick today, holding what you have lightly without ranking yourself against anyone else.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna it is better to walk his own path, even imperfectly, than to perform another's duty perfectly. You could today notice one small task that actually fits your own rhythm, letting it stand without measuring it against a batchmate's highlight reel. This keeps you on your own path, again.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Doing your own work well can be your worship of the source of all life.
verse_text.translation: By worshipping, through his own work, Him from whom all beings arise and by whom all this is pervaded, a person attains perfection.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that doing your own work well can be your worship of the source of all life. When comparison drains your peace, you could try giving your current task your full attention as a quiet offering, without measuring it against anyone else's path. Your work itself becomes the place where you meet what moves through everything.

story.title: The mongoose and the handful of flour
story.summary: At the end of Yudhishthira's grand horse sacrifice, a mongoose appeared with one side of its body made of gold. It declared that the whole sacrifice was worth less than a handful of flour. Once, it said, during a famine, a poor gleaner and his family each gave their last share of flour to a hungry guest. When the mongoose rolled in the flour that had spilled, half its body turned gold. It had gone to many great sacrifices since, hoping to turn the other half, and none had done it.
story.lesson: A small gift, honestly earned and given from little, outweighs the grandest show.

days.reading: The Mahabharata tells of a mongoose whose half-body turned gold because a poor family gave their last handful of flour to a hungry guest. It then visited Yudhishthira’s grand sacrifice and found it worth less than that small gift. Your peace is not measured by how you stack up against batchmates or cousins, but by the honest value of what you already give from where you are.

verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people worship him: those in distress, those seeking knowledge, those seeking wealth, and the wise. After walking away from a bad accident with just a few stitches, your mornings already feel like a gift. This verse invites you to wonder at the plain, self-respecting life you now hold rather than take it for granted.

verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You took money from your parents' savings for your startup and lost it all, and their silence makes it heavier. Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against their will, as if pushed by force. Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger, and this desire is the enemy that clouds wisdom like smoke over fire. He tells Arjuna to master it rather than let it master him. Your guilt sits in the gap between what you wanted for your startup and the loss you now carry. The verse names that gap without calling you wicked.

It points to the moment of temper itself, the flash that happened years ago, and lets you sit with that without turning it into a sentence about your whole life.

verse_text.speaker: Sutikshna
verse_text.setting: The young sage Sutikshna hears Ram is coming and runs to meet him, full of doubt about himself.
verse_text.line: I have no devotion, no wisdom, no steady love. But he loves the one who has nowhere else to go.
verse_text.translation: 'Will Ram, my master, with his brother, meet me as he would his own servant? There is no firm trust in my heart; no devotion, detachment or wisdom in my mind; no good company, no yoga, chanting or sacrifice, no steady love for his lotus feet. But the ocean of compassion has one habit: the one who has no other refuge is dear to him.'

reading: You feel like a thief every day because you lied on your CV to get this job, yet it is going well. Sutikshna says he has no devotion, no wisdom, no steady love, but the one who has nowhere else to go is dear. Your honest sense of not having enough to show is itself enough to be met with acceptance today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.
verse_text.line: Even if you were the worst wrongdoer of all, the raft of wisdom would carry you across.
verse_text.translation: Even if you are the most sinful of all sinners, you will cross over all wrongdoing by the raft of knowledge alone.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that even if you were the worst wrongdoer of all, the raft of knowledge would carry you across all wrongdoing. This speaks to the weight you feel when your wife shows kindness, as if the past still defines you. The verse sees this burden coming from a place where guilt feels like a permanent identity, yet it promises that true understanding can ferry you across the sea of what you did, leaving the river behind you.

verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.
verse_text.line: As a blazing fire turns wood to ash, real understanding burns away the hold of past actions.
verse_text.translation: As a blazing fire reduces fuel to ashes, Arjuna, so the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that as a blazing fire turns wood to ash, real understanding burns away the hold of past actions. The affair happened, and its effects still move through your life. What this burns is the grip of replaying it, the weight that makes her kindness feel like a burden, leaving you standing on the ground of what actually remains.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on simple, wholehearted devotion.
verse_text.line: Even if you've done great wrong, the moment you turn wholeheartedly, count yourself among the good.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that even someone who has done great wrong, the moment they turn wholeheartedly, should be counted among the good because their resolve is right. This speaks to the weight you carry when your wife is kind, since your past does not shut the door on who you are now. Let this ground you: your resolve today is what counts, not the record you cannot undo.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on simple, wholehearted devotion.
verse_text.line: Such a person soon turns good and finds lasting peace. Mark it: no one devoted to me is ever lost.
verse_text.translation: He soon becomes righteous and attains lasting peace. Kaunteya, declare it boldly: my devotee never perishes.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that someone who turns wholeheartedly soon becomes righteous and finds lasting peace, and declares boldly that his devotee is never lost. You carry the weight of a choice years ago that you cannot undo, yet this verse points to how a sincere turn can reshape who you are. You could let your wife’s kindness today remind you that you are not defined by that past, and simply sit with her without trying to earn her forgiveness.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna's final counsel: act with devotion, reflect, choose, and take refuge.
verse_text.line: Lean on me alone. I will free you from every wrong. Don't worry.
verse_text.translation: Abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in me alone. I will free you from all sins; do not grieve.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to abandon all dharmas and take refuge in him alone, promising to free him from every sin and bidding him not to grieve. For you, this invites setting down the weight you carry each time your wife is kind, trusting that release from fault does not erase your responsibility. You could try resting in that promise for one quiet moment today before responding to her next kindness.

story.title: Yudhishthira after the war
story.summary: Yudhishthira won the war and could not bear it. So many of his own family were dead, and he blamed himself. He wanted to give up the throne and go into the forest for good. One after another, his brothers, Draupadi, and the sages Devasthana and Vyasa argued with him about duty, guilt, grief and the shortness of life. Slowly he agreed to stay and rule, and to spend what was left of his life doing good.
story.lesson: Guilt and grief are real, but they are not the end. The good you do next counts.

days.reading: Yudhishthira won the war yet could not bear it, blaming himself for the dead and wanting to vanish into the forest. Your own weight carries a similar heaviness after what you did, yet the story shows that guilt does not have to be the final chapter. What you do next, even while the past remains, is what slowly steadies the throne.

meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even when they do not want to, as if pushed by force. Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger, and this anger clouds wisdom like smoke over fire. The verse proposes that one can master this force by seeing it clearly. You spoke a cruel joke about your classmate's family, and the memory still sits with you. This verse names the push behind actions you did not want to take.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You have found weeks of steady calm where traffic and deadlines no longer get under your skin. Krishna says the one whose happiness, delight and light are all within becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman. You can let this inner ease keep growing, trusting that your gladness does not have to wait for the next calm week to show up.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly. He describes the wise person who is equal-eyed toward all beings and does not sway between elation and despair. Such a person finds joy within, sees that sense pleasures end in sorrow, and withstands desire and anger. The verse proposes that one whose happiness, delight, and light all come from within attains the peace of Brahman while still living. You are already tasting this calm. It shows that the steadiness you feel does not have to depend on the week staying quiet.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.

reading: Krishna describes someone whose happiness, pleasure and light are all inside: antaḥ-sukhaḥ, antar-ārāmaḥ, antar-jyotiḥ. Good days still come from outside. This joy doesn't depend on them.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You feel a lightness in your chest these days and want to learn how to make it stay. The poet wonders what generous austerity ripened into the simple gifts of freedom, honest food, good company, and a mind that stirs only gently. This sense of wonder at what you already have can become a quiet practice, returning your attention to that same lightness in your chest.
meaning: The poet Bhartrihari speaks to the reader from his worship of Shiva. He then lists the goods of a simple, renunciant life. He wonders what generous austerity ripened into this freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, and a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long. meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while describing the wise person who has realised the highest truth. Arjuna has been asking about the nature of the one who sees clearly. Krishna says that the person whose happiness, delight and light all come from within becomes one with the ultimate reality and reaches its peace, even while still living in the world. Since your gladness already rests in you rather than in outer things, you might simply rest with that inner light as it is today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna sorts knowledge, action, doers, judgement, resolve and happiness by the three qualities.
verse_text.line: Some pleasure tastes like nectar at first and poison in the end. Know which kind you're choosing.
verse_text.translation: The happiness that comes from contact of the senses with their objects, like nectar at first and like poison in the end, is called rajasic.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that sensory pleasure tastes like nectar at first and like poison in the end. This is the rajasic kind, which fades and leaves loss behind. You already feel a quiet joy within, so today you can simply notice which pleasures leave you empty afterward, and which ones deepen the peace you carry.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Unhooked from outside pleasures, you find a joy within that doesn't run out.
verse_text.translation: One whose self is unattached to outer contacts finds the happiness that is in the self. Joined to Brahman by yoga, he enjoys undying happiness.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that when the self is unattached to outer contacts, it finds a joy within that does not run out. This speaks to the inner delight you already sense, the quiet gladness that asks to be known more deeply. Rest in this steady happiness that grows as it rests on itself alone.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: When the mind clears, sorrows start to dissolve, and understanding settles quickly.
verse_text.translation: In that clarity all sorrows come to an end; for one whose mind is clear, understanding soon becomes steady.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that when the mind clears, sorrows begin to dissolve and understanding settles quickly. This speaks to your peaceful inner state, where a quiet mind already makes room for steady gladness. Rest in this clarity today, letting understanding settle without forcing anything.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna sorts knowledge, action, doers, judgement, resolve and happiness by the three qualities.
verse_text.line: Some joy tastes like poison at first and like nectar in the end. That joy is worth it.
verse_text.translation: That which is like poison at first and like nectar in the end, born from the clarity of one's own understanding, is called sattvic happiness.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that some joy tastes like poison at first and like nectar in the end, born from clear understanding. You could sit quietly today and notice one small practice that feels effortful yet opens inward. This is the steady sweetness you already sense within, waiting to deepen.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on three kinds of food, effort, speech and giving.
verse_text.line: A calm mind, gentleness, quiet, self-restraint and a clean heart: that is discipline of mind.
verse_text.translation: Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint and purity of feeling: this is called austerity of the mind.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the austerity of mind is a calm, gentle, quiet, self-restrained and sincere heart. You already feel a quiet joy within, and today you could let that settle by sitting in silence for a few minutes and noticing any harsh thought before it becomes a word. This keeps the inner light steady without forcing anything.

story.title: Bhushunda
story.summary: The sage Vasishtha travelled to a wish-fulfilling tree on Mount Meru to meet Bhushunda, a crow who had watched whole ages of the world come and go and was still happy. Asked his secret, Bhushunda listed his habits. He didn't brood on the past or the future. He didn't fret about what he'd get next. Learning never made him proud. And he was glad when others were glad, and sad when they were sad.
story.lesson: A long, glad life comes from staying present, wanting little and staying kind.

days.reading: Vasishtha tells of Bhushunda, a crow who outlived whole ages yet stayed happy. He did not brood on what passed or fret over what comes next. You already feel a quiet joy within and wish to know it more; this story shows that simply resting in the present, wanting little, and staying kind is how gladness lasts.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You eat alone in the dining hall while others sit in their groups. Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever sees him in everything and everything in him is never lost to him, and he is never lost to them. Even when you are far from home and surrounded by people with their own circles, this bond stays present in the ordinary moments around you, including the next meal you take.
meaning: Krishna speaks this to Arjuna while teaching him how to meditate and what a settled mind looks like. Arjuna has been hearing about the yogi who sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self. Krishna restates that idea in his own voice. He says that whoever sees him everywhere and sees everything resting in him will never be lost to him, and he will never be lost to that person. You are far from home and eating alone while others sit in their groups. This verse says that the bond you seek is already present in the ordinary moments around you, including the next meal you take.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You stay at home in a new country while your husband works long hours, and some days pass without another adult to speak to. Krishna tells Arjuna that he who sees him everywhere and everything in him is never lost to him, and he is never lost to that person. On a quiet day like this, the verse names a bond that distance cannot break: you are seen, and you are not lost.
meaning: Krishna speaks this to Arjuna while teaching him how to meditate and what a settled mind looks like. He tells Arjuna that whoever sees him in every place and sees every place resting within him will never be separated from him, and he will never be separated from that person. You are raising children in a place that still feels foreign, while your husband is away at work. The verse names a bond that no empty room or long day can undo.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna tells Arjuna where the divine is found.
verse_text.line: The divine lives in the heart of every being, yours included.
verse_text.translation: The Lord dwells in the heart of every being, Arjuna, moving all beings by his power as if mounted on a machine.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the Lord dwells in the heart of every being, including yours. You do not have to wait for another adult to speak to first; this presence is already inside you, right here in this flat and city. Let that inner dwelling be the ground you stand on today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna tells Arjuna who he is to every being.
verse_text.line: I am your goal, your support, your witness, your home, your shelter and your friend.
verse_text.translation: I am the goal, the sustainer, the master, the witness, the home, the refuge and the friend; the origin and the dissolution, the ground, the treasure-house and the undying seed.

days.reading: In one verse Krishna lists what he is to every being: goal, support, witness, home (nivāsaḥ), shelter (śaraṇam) and friend (suhṛt). If you've been missing all of those, this verse names them together.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, briefly describing meditation and the peace it brings.
verse_text.line: The divine is the well-wisher of every being, you included. Knowing this, you find peace.
verse_text.translation: Knowing me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great lord of all the worlds, and the friend of all beings, one attains peace.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the divine is the selfless friend and well-wisher of every being, and knowing this brings peace. You may go days without speaking to another adult, yet this presence wishes you well all the same, without expecting anything back. Let that quiet steadiness be a ground beneath your feet this evening.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Feel others' joy and pain as if they were your own. That is the highest practice.
verse_text.translation: One who, by comparison with himself, sees the same everywhere, Arjuna, whether in pleasure or in pain, is considered the highest yogi.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to feel others' joy and pain as if they were his own; that is the highest practice. You could try this today with one person you meet—a neighbour, a shopkeeper, or a fellow parent—by noticing one small thing about their day and letting it register as real. This turns your attention outward, the way the verse suggests connection begins.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, describing the qualities of the person dear to God.
verse_text.line: Hate no one. Be friendly and kind, free of 'mine' and ego, steady in pain and joy, and forgiving.
verse_text.translation: One who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free from possessiveness and ego, even in pain and pleasure, and forgiving,

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to hate no one, to be friendly and compassionate, free from possessiveness and ego, steady through pain and joy, and forgiving. You could offer one small kindness to another adult today, even without expecting anything back. This does not ask you to ignore harm or stay where you are unsafe; it simply points to a steady openness you can hold.

story.title: Ram and Sugriva become friends
story.summary: Ram had lost his home, and his wife Sita had been taken. Sugriva, driven out by his brother, had lost his home and his wife too. They met in the forest and swore friendship before a fire. Then Sugriva brought out the jewels Sita had dropped as she was carried away. Ram broke down at the sight of them, and Sugriva, who had his own grief, comforted him: in trouble, think it through steadily, and lean on your friend.
story.lesson: Two people in trouble can carry each other.

days.reading: In the Kishkindha Kanda, Ram and Sugriva, both driven from home and grieving lost wives, meet in the forest and swear friendship before a fire. Sugriva then comforts Ram, who breaks down seeing Sita’s dropped jewels, telling him to steady his mind and lean on his friend. This shows that two people in trouble can carry each other, which may reach you on days when long hours leave you without another adult to speak to.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: With both sons settled outside and the two of you here alone, the days feel hard to bear. Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever sees him everywhere and everything in him is never lost to him, and he is never lost to them. When the house feels quiet and the afternoon stretches long, this can mean that no distance can break the bond that keeps you held in sight.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield while teaching him the nature of meditation and a settled mind. He tells Arjuna that whoever sees him everywhere and sees everything resting in him will never be lost to him, and he will never be lost to that person. The verse proposes that a steady awareness which finds the divine in all things and all things in the divine creates a bond that distance cannot break. With both sons settled far away and the two of you here alone, the quiet days can feel endless. Krishna speaks of a bond that no distance breaks, so the quiet does not have to mean you are cast out.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You are flying to Doha this Sunday for your first job abroad, carrying hope with you. Lakshmana tells Ram that enthusiasm is powerful, and for the one who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach. Your own resolve can carry you through the new city and role ahead.
meaning: At Lake Pampa in spring, Rama is sunk in grief after Sita has been taken. Every bird and mated deer around him only sharpens his longing. Lakshman sees this despair and tells him that enthusiasm is powerful. There is no strength greater than it. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach. The verse proposes that resolute energy is the root of all effort, and by it alone the brothers can recover Sita. You are about to cross into a new country for work, and hope is already moving in you. Lakshman's words suggest that this forward pull itself is a form of strength that can carry you through the unknown ahead.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Don't abandon work that suits you just because it has flaws. Every undertaking has some, like fire has smoke.
verse_text.translation: One should not give up the work suited to one's nature, Kaunteya, even if it has faults; for all undertakings are clouded by faults, as fire is by smoke.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that every undertaking is clouded by faults, just as fire is by smoke, so do not abandon work suited to you merely because it has flaws. Your first job abroad will also carry its own smoke, and that is simply how any new beginning starts. When Sunday brings you to Doha, notice the work itself and keep moving through what does not yet fit perfectly.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Without self-control it's hard. With sincere effort and the right means, it's within reach.
verse_text.translation: Yoga is hard to reach for one whose self is uncontrolled, in my view. But one whose self is controlled and who strives can reach it by the right means.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that yoga is hard for the uncontrolled, yet with sincere effort and the right means it is within reach. As you begin this first job abroad, the steadiness to see it through is already possible through your own striving. Let the work of arriving in Doha on Sunday be your right means, one step at a time.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: So keep doing the work that needs doing, well and without clinging. That's how you rise.
verse_text.translation: Therefore, always do the work that has to be done, without attachment; by working without attachment a person reaches the highest.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to keep doing the work that needs doing, well and without clinging. For you, this means showing up steadily in Doha, letting the routine carry you rather than gripping the result. The work itself becomes the ground beneath your feet.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.
verse_text.line: Cut the doubt in your heart with clear understanding, then stand up and act.
verse_text.translation: Therefore, cutting with the sword of knowledge this doubt in your heart born of ignorance, take refuge in yoga, and stand up, Bharata.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to cut the doubt in his heart with clear understanding, then stand up and act. As you fly to doha for your first job abroad, some uncertainty is natural. You could write down one fact you know is true about this step, then take the next small action today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna, as Time, tells Arjuna the outcome is already set and urges him to act.
verse_text.line: It's already set in motion. Rise and do your part; be the instrument.
verse_text.translation: Therefore stand up and win glory; conquer your enemies and enjoy a prosperous kingdom. They have already been slain by me; be merely the instrument, ambidextrous archer.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the larger outcome is already moving, and urges him to rise and play his part as the instrument. You are flying to do this new chapter on Sunday, so you could simply show up and do the first task without carrying the weight of making everything succeed alone. Let the bigger story carry what is beyond your reach, while you step into what is right in front of you.

story.title: Satyakama Jabala
story.summary: Young Satyakama wanted to study, but he didn't know his father's lineage. He told the teacher exactly what his mother had told him. The teacher accepted him for that honesty and handed him four hundred weak, thin cows to look after. Satyakama said he wouldn't come back until they were a thousand. He spent years in the forest, and returned with a thousand cows and a mind that nature itself had taught.
story.lesson: Start honestly, start small, and stay with it.

days.reading: In the Chhandogya Upanishad, the teacher accepts the young Satyakama simply because he speaks the truth about not knowing his father, then sends him to tend four hundred thin cows. You are beginning a first job abroad, and this story shows that starting with honest uncertainty and a small, fragile step is enough. Stay with the work until it grows into a thousand.

story.title: Pingala's song
story.summary: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira about Pingala, who sat awake one night waiting for a lover who never came. Every sound outside might have been his footsteps, so she kept listening. Late in the night she saw what was keeping her awake. It was her hope that someone else would arrive and settle her. She let that hope go, and she slept peacefully.
story.lesson: Letting go of an expectation can bring the sleep that waiting never will.

days.reading: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira about Pingala, who stayed awake waiting for a lover who never came, only to realize her sleeplessness came from the hope that someone else would arrive and settle her. verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You are wound up like a spring through audit season, working till midnight. Krishna tells Arjuna that contact with the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain, which come and go and do not last. You can bear this tightness patiently, knowing the season itself has an end.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna reminds him that the true self never begins and never ends. Yet the body feels contact with the world. That contact brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These feelings arrive and then they leave. They do not stay forever. Krishna asks Arjuna to endure them without surrendering to either joy or sorrow. The audit season has wound you tight through midnight hours. That restlessness is a passing contact between your senses and the work, not the whole of who you are.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: With midterms, work shifts, and club deadlines pressing in, your shoulders have lifted toward your ears. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go through contact with the world, and he asks us to bear them as they pass. This means your tightness can move through you without becoming the whole of you. Let your shoulders drop again when the next shift ends.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield, just after telling him that the true self passes through childhood, youth and old age unchanged. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna says that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These arrive and depart by nature. They do not last. You could bear them without letting either joy or grief carry you away. What you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain. Your body is holding the weight of midterms, shifts and deadlines right now. The tightness in your shoulders can move through you without becoming who you are.

You can notice the racing heart as a contact that arrives and will pass, without letting it decide the whole of your day. When the phone buzzes this weekend, you might let that sensation move through you like a brief current.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that the true self never dies and never is born. Yet the body meets cold and heat, pleasure and pain through the senses. These sensations come and go. They do not last. A person must bear them with patience and not be swept away by either joy or grief.

meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. The pressure from your karigar, supplier and client is real right now. It will move through you like weather and leave, because it is not the whole of who you are.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You feel wound up because your plate is overflowing and demands keep piling on. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born, and from attachment comes desire, which blocked turns into anger. Right now, that buildup shows up in your mind as a knot you cannot think past. Notice the moment your attention locks onto what is demanded before the snap comes.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after Arjuna asks what a person of steady mind looks like in speech, sitting and walking. Krishna has just warned that the senses can carry away even a wise person's mind. Now he traces the inner chain. When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire, and when that desire is blocked, anger arises. Steadiness is built by guarding where the attention rests, because anger starts with what a person keeps dwelling on. Your plate is full and the demands keep coming. That buildup can turn into anger when your mind keeps returning to what is being asked of you before the snap arrives.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse_text.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

reading: With everything feeling urgent in your first job, Krishna tells Arjuna that your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits, and not to cling to doing nothing. That means the pressure you feel does not include owning the outcome. You can give your full attention to the effort right now, and let the result be what it will be.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is afraid to fight. Krishna tells him that a person has a right only to the action itself. The results belong to something else. The work must be done fully. The outcome must not be clung. In plain modern words, do your part and let go of owning what comes after. In your first job, the pressure to perform can feel like it owns you. This verse separates the effort from the outcome, so the urgency does not have to crush you.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

meaning: King Bali has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day he sits by his window and notices that day follows night, and the same tasks return without end. He speaks to himself and says that to a thinking person this repetition feels like a mockery. The verse proposes that when life becomes a loop, the way out is not more work but mastering the mind that runs the loop. Your restaurant in December runs on the same loop of orders and noise. The verse names that loop without asking you to walk away from it.

Yet the body feels contact with the world, and this brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These feelings come and go. They do not last. Arjuna must learn to bear them without being swept away. Your body is caught in a current of demands that feel endless right now. The verse names this pull as something that arises and passes, not as a fixed state that defines you.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna, seeing his own family in the enemy ranks, collapses in grief before the battle.
verse_text.line: Shaking limbs, a dry mouth, a racing body: the Gita opens with a panic attack, not a hero.
verse_text.translation: My limbs give way, my mouth is parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.

reading: You feel targets rising while your team shrinks, and you do not know how to keep up. In the Gita, Arjuna tells Krishna that his limbs give way, his mouth is parched, his body trembles, and his hair stands on end. That same shaking and dry mouth can be present for you today when work feels unsafe, naming the body's honest response without asking you to fix it right away. Notice where your own hands or breath are right now.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield just before the war begins. He sees his own teachers, uncles, sons and friends standing in the enemy ranks. His body reacts to the sight. His limbs give way, his mouth is parched, his body trembles and his hair stands on end. The verse proposes that even the strongest people can freeze. The Gita begins with a breakdown, not with a hero. Your targets keep rising while your team keeps shrinking, and your body may carry the same honest shock that Arjuna felt when the ground fell away.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.

reading: You face daily pressure with two years left before retirement, carrying the biggest project of your career. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go, and do not last. You can bear this contact of the senses with its objects patiently, without being swept away by the pressure itself.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield after Arjuna has laid down his weapons in grief. He tells him that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These states arise and pass away by their very nature. They do not last. So Arjuna must bear them patiently, without letting either joy or grief carry him away. The pressure you carry at work has a shape that changes. It is not the whole of who you are, and it will not stay fixed forever.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: You mentioned that people already treat you differently since becoming partner, and that you like it a bit too much. Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is the one the world follows. Your conduct now quietly sets the tone for those around you, so carrying your new standing with steadiness speaks louder than the shift in how others treat you.
meaning: Krishna speaks this to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna has been wondering why anyone should keep working when they have already found peace. Krishna answers that even those who are fulfilled act for the sake of the world. Whatever a respected person does, others copy. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows. The verse says that people take their cue from those they look up. So anyone with standing is responsible for the standard their conduct sets. You now carry a new weight at the firm. The way you move through the office sets a quiet example for those around you.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You want to remain the person who began in a dorm room now that your app has crossed a million downloads. The poet says he does not know what generous austerity ripened into this freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, good company, and a mind that stirs only gently. You can hold that same wonder today at the quiet dignity you still carry, choosing your own hours and honest food, letting the milestone simply deepen your gratitude for the calm you started with.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines to the reader from his Worship of Shiva. He has just noted that moonlight, poetry and good company lose their charm once the mind sees how fleeting they are, and that the wise leave palaces for the forest. He now lists the goods of a simple life.

Others look to that example. So the conduct of a leading person becomes the rule for everyone around them. Your raise has put you in view. verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, listing the qualities that free us and those that bind.
verse_text.line: Show-off, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance: the marks of a nature heading the wrong way.
verse_text.translation: Hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance belong to one born with the demonic nature, Partha.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance mark a nature heading the wrong way. After your recent promotions, these tendencies can quietly grow when people start looking to you for advice. Notice if your speech turns sharp or if you begin to perform rather than simply act.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks how one beyond the three qualities lives; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Even in pain and pleasure, at ease in yourself; earth, stone and gold the same; praise and blame alike.
verse_text.translation: who is the same in pain and pleasure, at home in the self, to whom a clod, a stone and gold are alike, who is the same to the pleasant and the unpleasant, steady, the same in blame and praise,

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the one who rests in the self treats a lump of earth, a stone and gold as the same, and meets praise and blame alike. With your recent promotions bringing people to you for advice, this steadiness offers you ground to stand on beyond the hype. Let the clod, the stone and the gold pass through without shifting who you are.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the body as a field, and what true knowledge consists of.
verse_text.line: No need for status, no pretence, no harm, patience, straightness, respect for teachers, purity, steadiness, self-control.
verse_text.translation: Humility, freedom from pretence, non-violence, patience, uprightness, service of the teacher, purity, steadiness and self-control,

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that true knowledge begins with humility, freedom from pretence, and patience. With people now coming to you for advice after your recent promotions, this points to staying grounded in who you are rather than in the attention you receive. Let your steadiness show in how you answer them today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna sorts knowledge, action, doers, judgement, resolve and happiness by the three qualities.
verse_text.line: Free of clinging and boasting, full of resolve and enthusiasm, unchanged by success or failure: the best kind of doer.
verse_text.translation: The doer who is free from attachment, does not speak of himself, is full of steadiness and enthusiasm, and unmoved by success or failure, is called sattvic.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the best doer acts with full resolve and enthusiasm yet stays free from clinging and boasting, unmoved by success or failure. You have stepped into a place where people seek your counsel after two promotions, and this steadiness offers a way to keep your drive without letting praise become your measure. You could pause before your next meeting to notice one task you are doing simply for its own sake, not for the credit.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: The wise see the same self in a scholar, a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcast.
verse_text.translation: The wise see with an equal eye a learned and humble Brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and one who eats dog-meat.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the wise see the same self in a scholar, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcast. After your recent promotions, you could treat the colleague who reports to you and the newest intern with the exact same regard today. Let this equal eye guide how you listen, without letting success change who you value.

story.title: Nahusha's fall
story.summary: King Nahusha was so successful that he was made ruler of heaven. Drunk on it, he made sages carry his palanquin and kicked one to hurry him along. The sage cursed him, and he fell to earth as a giant python. Ages later he seized Bhima in the forest, and was freed only after Yudhishthira answered his questions about what makes a person good.
story.lesson: Success can blind anyone. Conduct is what makes a person good.

days.reading: King Nahusha reached the pinnacle of success and was made ruler of heaven, yet he grew arrogant enough to kick a sage and was cursed to fall as a python. This shows how success can blind anyone, no matter how high they rise. You are navigating new visibility after two promotions, so let your conduct—not the hype—be what defines you.

Let that recognition sit with you as you close your laptop tonight.

He has done the same bathing, eating and sleeping, day after day, night after night. He feels mocked by the endless repetition. The verse proposes that when life feels like a loop, the work is not more of it but mastering the mind that runs it. You have spent nine years in the same job, waking tired and moving on autopilot until you crash at night. Bali names the absurdity you feel today: the loop has become visible to you.

verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: You have spent three years moving between consulting assignments four days a week, and now your body is exhausted in a way a long weekend cannot fix. Bali, sitting by his window, says again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks, and to a thinking person this feels like a mockery. Your own repetition may carry that same weight today, as the same cycle returns without relief.
meaning: Bali, a king who has ruled the three worlds for ages, sits by his window and wonders what his endless reign adds up to. He sees the same bathing, eating and sleeping, day after day, night after night. He remembers a riddle his father Virochana once told him. The riddle speaks of a vast realm ruled by a silent king and an all-powerful minister. The minister is the mind. Bali realises that winning the mind over, by practice, is what wins everything. The verse captures his weariness at this endless round. Your body knows this loop after three years of travel. The verse names the mockery you feel when the same chain returns without relief.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.

verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: Eight years running your clinic alone, with no proper holidays, has left you feeling like a shell. Bali says, day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over, and a thinking person feels mocked by it. That sense of mockery speaks to the autopilot you are on today. You might let the verse sit beside the clinic door as a quiet witness to the cycle you are in.
meaning: The demon king Bali speaks this to himself while sitting alone at his window. He has ruled the three worlds for ages. The same duties repeat without change. He feels that this endless loop mocks any thinking person who looks for meaning in it. Your clinic has run on the same rhythm for eight years. The verse names the weariness of that loop without calling your work worthless.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'On the Greatness of Time'.
verse_text.line: Same night, same day, the same tasks on repeat. We run in circles and call it living.
verse_text.translation: Thinking 'it is the same night again, the same day', creatures run about in vain, busy as ever with the tasks they have set going; with work full of the same repeated things, tormented by this round of existence, alas, out of delusion we feel no shame.

reading: You dread logging in after only two years because the days feel like a loop. Bhartrihari writes that creatures run in circles with the same night, same day, and same tasks, calling it living. This verse names that repetition without blaming you for it. Today, you might notice one small shift in how you begin your morning, so the day is not simply a rerun.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines from his poem on the greatness of Time. He addresses the reader who is caught in endless routine. At the moment he speaks, he sees creatures trapped in a cycle where every night and every day blur into identical tasks. He points out that they run about busily with the same work they started, yet they do not feel shame at how time slips away while they repeat the same motions. He asks us to notice that life is passing while we stay busy with stale pursuits. Your dread at logging in comes from days that feel identical. The verse names that loop without calling it your fault.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You work 12-hour shifts in short staffing and feel numb both at work and at home. The Yoga Vasishtha describes someone who no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work, but simply keeps silent. This withdrawal is noticed and taken seriously by those around him, who bring help rather than scolding. Let someone in your life do that for you today.
meaning: In the Yoga Vasishtha, a servant reports to King Dasharatha about Rama. Rama has just returned from a long pilgrimage. He no longer eats properly, avoids company, and calls everything unreal. The servant adds that Rama no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He simply keeps silent. The text treats this withdrawal as a serious state that calls for care and conversation, not scolding.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

verse_text.speaker: Vibhishan
verse_text.setting: Vibhishan, Ravana's good-hearted brother, describes his life in Ravana's court.
verse_text.line: I live here like the tongue among the teeth.
verse_text.translation: Son of the wind, hear how I live: like the poor tongue among the teeth. Friend, knowing me to be without support, will the Lord of the Sun dynasty ever show me grace?

reading: It sounds like home doesn't feel safe right now.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna, seeing his own family in the enemy ranks, collapses in grief before the battle.
verse_text.line: Shaking limbs, a dry mouth, a racing body: the Gita opens with a panic attack, not a hero.
verse_text.translation: My limbs give way, my mouth is parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.

reading: Your body is reacting to sudden uncertainty. In the Gita, Arjuna tells Krishna that his limbs give way, his mouth is parched, his body trembles, and his hair stands on end. This mirrors the physical surge you may be feeling right now as you face the next sixty days. You might notice your own hands shaking or your throat tightening when you think about what comes next.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He has asked Krishna to drive the chariot between the two armies. There he sees his teachers, uncles, sons, grandsons and friends standing in the enemy ranks. His body reacts before his mind can catch up. He tells Krishna that his limbs give way, his mouth is parched, his body trembles and his hair stands on end. The verse proposes that even a capable person can be overtaken by the body when the ground shifts beneath them. Your own body is sounding the same alarm right now as the next sixty days take shape.

It proposes that even the strongest people freeze. The Gita begins with a breakdown, not a hero. Your body is doing exactly what Arjuna's did when safety at work suddenly felt out of reach. That shaking is not a sign that you are weak or wrong.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You are facing a mortgage, two kids, and only one income now after being made redundant. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. This verse names the moment of putting everything down when you cannot go on, and the story moves forward from there.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. Arjuna has just argued that killing his own kin is a ruinous wrong, and that he would rather die unarmed. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna sinks onto the chariot seat, letting his bow and arrows fall, his mind overcome by grief. The verse marks the lowest point before any teaching begins. It shows a strong man frozen, not by cowardice, but by the weight of what he faces. You are in that same frozen moment, with the mortgage and the two children and the sudden silence where a second income used to be.
