verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: Krishna calls these mātrā-sparśa: contacts, things that touch you and move on. A deadline, a bad week, a hard meeting. They hurt while they last, they pass, and Krishna asks you to bear them (titikṣasva) until they do.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Without inner discipline there's no clarity; without clarity, no peace; and without peace, where is happiness?
verse_text.translation: For the undisciplined there is no understanding and no steady contemplation. Without contemplation there is no peace, and for the one without peace, where is happiness?

days.reading: Krishna lays out a chain. An unsettled mind has no clarity, without clarity there is no peace, and without peace there is no happiness, however good things look on paper. The workload is one part of stress. The other part is a mind with no place to stand.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on working in the world without being stained by it.
verse_text.line: Like a lotus leaf in water, do your work without letting the mess soak in.
verse_text.translation: One who acts offering all actions to the Supreme, giving up attachment, is not touched by wrong, as a lotus leaf is not wet by water.

days.reading: A lotus leaf sits in water all its life, and the water still beads and rolls off it. Krishna uses it for someone who works fully and lets the mess around them roll off. You stay in the pond and keep your surface dry.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Rivers pour into the ocean and it stays full and still. Let desires enter you the same way.
verse_text.translation: As waters enter the ocean, which is ever being filled yet stays unmoved within its shores, so the one into whom all desires enter in the same way finds peace, not the one who craves desires.

days.reading: Rivers keep pouring into the ocean and it stays full and still. Demands will keep coming. In Krishna's picture, peace comes from being deep enough to take them in.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Moderate in food and rest, in work and play, in sleep and waking: that's how sorrow eases.
verse_text.translation: For one who is moderate in food and recreation, measured in effort at work, moderate in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.

days.reading: This is the Gita at its most practical. Krishna tells Arjuna that the yoga which ends sorrow belongs to someone moderate in food, movement, work, sleep and waking. A lot of stress starts as a schedule with no rest built into it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on acting free of ego, like and dislike, in your own way.
verse_text.line: Hand your work to something higher, drop the 'mine' and the hoping, and act with the fever gone.
verse_text.translation: Surrendering all actions to me, with your mind on the inner self, free from hope and the sense of 'mine', fight with your fever gone.

days.reading: The Sanskrit is vigata-jvaraḥ: with the fever gone. Krishna still wants Arjuna to fight, and to fight without the heat of 'mine' and anxious hoping. Offer the work to something larger than your worry, and do it.

story.title: Janaka on the palace roof
story.summary: Walking in his garden one spring, King Janaka overheard hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbed to his palace roof and questioned everything he had lived for. When his attendant came to call him to the day's work, he could have walked away from the throne. He didn't. He went back and did his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutched.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

days.reading: When stress builds, it's tempting to dream of quitting everything. Janaka kept the same work and held it differently.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.
verse_text.line: Quiet, you're dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga.
verse_text.translation: Keep quiet and you are dumb; speak well and you are a babbler or a windbag; stay close and you are pushy; keep away and you lack confidence; be patient and you are a coward; refuse to put up with things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis.

reading: You are working and feel hurt. Bhartrihari tells you that serving a boss is harder than yoga: keep quiet and you are dull, speak up and you are a show-off, be patient and you are weak. The verse shows that when you serve someone powerful, any behaviour can be read as a fault. Today, your report being lifted up before everyone and called bakwas sits inside that impossible position, not inside you.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines from his Nitishatakam as a field guide to wicked people. He is describing the courtier who serves a cruel master. No matter what the servant does, the master twists it into a fault. Stay silent and you are dull. Speak and you are a windbag. Stay close and you are pushy. Keep away and you lack confidence. Be patient and you are weak. Refuse and you are ill bred. Serving another in this way is a duty so deep that even yogis cannot fathom it. Your boss turned your report into a fault in front of everyone. The verse shows that when you serve someone powerful, any behaviour can be read as a fault. That impossible position is not a measure of you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.

reading: A younger man from outside has been hired for the permanent role you were acting in. Krishna says it is better to walk your own path, imperfectly, than to perform another's duty well. Your two years of steady leadership count as your own path, not a failed copy of someone else's.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna stands between two armies, unsure whether to fight. Krishna tells him that each person has duties suited to their own nature. Doing the work that fits you, even with flaws, brings no fault. It is better to walk your own path imperfectly than to perform another person's duty perfectly. Your two years as acting head are your own path, not a failed copy of the permanent role. The verse asks you to see that fit honestly, without measuring yourself against the younger man.

meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines from the section on the wicked, addressing the reader who serves a master. He lays out a courtier's trap. Keep silent and you are dull. It is a double bind built into the room.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': the poet to his own hope.
verse_text.line: I swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. Hope, how much longer will you make me dance?
verse_text.translation: I somehow put up with the taunts of the wicked while trying to please them; I held back my tears and laughed with an empty heart; I folded my hands even before people whose minds were numbed by money. Hope, futile hope, how much more will you make me dance?

reading: You gave ten years and still the promotion went to someone else, feeling like you count for nothing here. Bhartrihari cries out to Hope itself, saying he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart, asking how much longer it will make him dance. Today, your own empty laughter after being passed over might be the weight you are carrying, and naming that cost is the first step toward deciding what comes next.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to his own hope from the censure of craving. He tells it he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. He folded his hands before people numbed by money. He asks how much longer hope will make him dance. The verse says we think we are chasing things, but really the chase is using up our lives.

reading: You notice that locals and westerners get the promotions while you do the work. Krishna says it is better to walk your own path imperfectly than to perform another's duty perfectly. Your own effort, even if overlooked right now, carries its own worth rather than copying someone else's track.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna stands between two armies, unsure whether to fight. Krishna has just explained that perfection comes from worshipping through one's own work. Now Krishna tells him that one's own duty, even if done imperfectly, is better than another's duty performed perfectly. Acting in line with one's own nature brings no fault. You do the work while others take the credit. Your own effort carries worth even when it looks overlooked beside someone else's polished track.

reading: You are angry that your biggest client pays months late and treats you like a nobody in front of his staff. Bhartrihari cries out to his own hope, saying he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart while trying to please the wicked. Today, you might recognise the same dance of swallowing your worth to keep the work flowing. The verse simply names that forced laughter, leaving you with the image of folded hands before those numbed by money.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines to his own hope from the Censure of Craving. He has spent his life digging for treasure, flattering kings, and crossing seas for gain. Now he lists the humiliations he swallowed to win favour from the wealthy and wicked. He held back his tears and laughed with an empty heart. He folded his hands before men whose minds were numbed by money. He asks how much longer hope will make him dance this servile dance. Your biggest client pays late and dismisses you before his staff. Bhartrihari names the same forced laughter and folded hands that come from hoping a powerful person will finally value you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: Krishna says his heart is churned like a fire-stick, and the harsh words his relatives speak keep burning him day after day. You heard your co-founder take all the credit in the investor meeting as if you had done nothing. This verse names that exact sting of being spoken over by someone close, and it shows that such words can keep burning long after they are said.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after he has grown tired of feuds within his own clan. He tells Narada that he gives his relatives half of what he owns and bears their harsh words, yet his heart is churned like a fire-stick being rubbed to kindle flame. The cruel words his kin speak keep burning him, day after day. The verse proposes that in family feuds, the only weapon that works is gentleness, patience and respect. Your co-founder spoke over you in front of investors and took the credit as if your work did not exist. This verse names that sting and shows it can keep burning long after the moment passes.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: You carry the ache of words never spoken at your wedding. Krishna tells Narada that harsh words from relatives keep burning him, day after day, his heart churned like a fire-stick. That same slow burn can live in you now, not because you failed, but because the wound was left open.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after growing weary of feuds inside his own clan. He admits that even though he gives his relatives half of what he owns, their harsh words still grind his heart like a fire-stick being churned for flame. The verse proposes that in family quarrels, gentleness, patience and respect are the only tools that work. Your father spoke about your brother at your wedding. That moment left the wound open, and now the absence of pride still aches.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You carry the hurt of being spoken about behind your back and left without a single defense. Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever sees him everywhere, and everything in him, is never lost to him, nor he to them. You might let this mean that even when your husband’s family reaches only for their own needs, you are not erased from sight by a presence that holds every moment you live, including the ones right here with your children.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the field. He has just described the yogi who sees the self in all beings. Now he restates this in his own voice. He says that whoever sees him everywhere and sees everything resting in him will never be lost to him, and he will never be lost to that person. The verse proposes that a steady gaze, returned to again and again, settles the mind. Even when your husband's family speaks about you in secret and your husband stays silent, you are still held in a sight that does not look away. That presence includes the life you are living with your children right now.

This verse names that same lingering sting from your own family, holding the truth that such words can keep burning long after they are spoken.

Krishna says his own relatives' harsh words churn his heart like fire-sticks, burning day after day. The verse names that exact sting of words from those closest to you, and it ends with the image of that fire still burning.

Your siblings are telling a story about your care for your mother that erases your sacrifice. The verse names the particular sting of words from those closest to you.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: You carry the anger of fifteen years spent sending money home. Ram speaks of a single sorrow that burns his heart: the king did not tell him the news himself. The deepest hurt can be that the one you loved avoided facing you directly, rather than the loss alone.
meaning: Ram speaks these words to Kaikeyi after he has calmly accepted fourteen years of exile in the forest. His father has agreed to send him away so that Bharata may be crowned. Ram shows no anger at the loss of a kingdom. He agrees at once. What wounds him is that the king did not come himself to say it. The hurt is not the news. It is that the one he loved did not face him and tell him directly.

verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.

The point is that in family quarrels the only weapon that works is gentleness, patience and respect.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has lain on the shore for three days asking the ocean for a way across. No answer comes.
verse_text.line: Calm, patience, honesty and kind words: people who don't value them will read them as weakness.
verse_text.translation: See the ocean's arrogance: he does not even show himself. Calm, forbearance, straightforwardness and gentle speech, these virtues of the good, are taken by the unworthy as signs of weakness.

days.reading: Ram tells Lakshman that calm patience, honesty and gentle speech are read as weakness by those who lack them, after the ocean ignores his three days of polite requests. Your hurt makes sense when kindness is treated as nothing. Today, notice that the misreading belongs to the other person, not to your own patience.

verse_text.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse_text.speaker: Prahlada (quoted by Draupadi)
verse_text.setting: Draupadi quotes old Prahlada answering his grandson: is forgiveness better, or force?
verse_text.line: Force isn't always right, and forgiveness isn't always right. Wisdom is knowing which the moment needs.
verse_text.translation: Force is not always best, and forgiveness is not always best. Know this for certain, my child: both have their place.

days.reading: Draupadi tells Yudhishthira that force is not always best, and forgiveness is not always best either; wisdom is knowing which the moment needs. This speaks to your hurt without asking you to carry a burden you never chose. You can stand on the ground that choosing a firm boundary today is its own wisdom, not a failure.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Uttanka, furious that the war happened, threatens to curse Krishna for not stopping it.
verse_text.line: I tried hard to make peace. When people refuse to be reconciled, you can't force it.
verse_text.translation: I made every effort earlier to bring the Kauravas to peace. But they could not be brought to agree, however I tried.

verse_text.speaker: Seer
verse_text.setting: The creation story: last of all, dharma is made.
verse_text.line: Nothing is higher than what is right. With it the weak can face the strong. What is right is truth.
verse_text.translation: Still he did not flourish. So he created a higher form, dharma. Dharma is the power over power; nothing is higher than dharma. Through dharma even a weak man can stand up to a strong one, as with the help of a king. That dharma is truth. So people say of one who speaks truth, 'He speaks dharma,' and of one who speaks dharma, 'He speaks truth.' Both are the same.

days.reading: The seer says that nothing is higher than what is right, and through it the weak can face the strong. What is right is truth. You could write down one true thing about your own effort today, letting what is right stand beside the harsh words, without trying to match force with force.

verse_text.speaker: Kabandha
verse_text.setting: Ram is lost and grieving; Kabandha tells him to seek Sugriva, who has also lost his wife and home.
verse_text.line: Find a friend who knows your kind of trouble. You won't get through this alone.
verse_text.translation: You must make him your friend, best of friends. Thinking it over, I see no success for you without it.

days.reading: In the Aranya Kanda, Kabandha tells Rama to make a friend who knows his kind of trouble, because without that bond success is not in sight. You could share one line of what you are carrying with a classmate who also feels weighed down. This does not erase your hurt, but it places one step of the burden beside someone who understands.

story.title: Hanuman finds a friend in Lanka
story.summary: Searching Lanka, Hanuman is surprised to find a house with Ram's name on it. Its owner, Vibhishan, Ravana's brother, says he lives in Lanka like a tongue among teeth. Hanuman tells him even a restless monkey like himself was given Ram's love.
story.lesson: Even in a hostile place there may be one ally; find them.

days.reading: In the Ramcharitmanas, Hanuman finds Ravana’s brother Vibhishan living inside Lanka like a tongue among teeth, unable to share his values with those around him. He admits he has no practice and no love for Ram’s feet, yet trusts that without Hari’s grace one does not meet a saint. This speaks to your hurt from harsh words, showing that even in a place where you cannot be fully open, one true meeting can bring rest beyond words.

reading: You feel like a stranger in your own home. Krishna says his heart is churned like a fire-stick, and the harsh words his relatives speak keep burning him day after day. Your mother-in-law’s criticism and your husband’s dismissal echo that same fire, still burning inside you now.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after years of feuding inside his own clan. He tells Narada that he gives his kin half of what he owns and bears their harsh words, yet those words grind his heart like someone churning a fire-stick. The verse proposes that in family conflict, the only weapon that works is gentleness, patience and respect. Your mother-in-law speaks against you before your children and your husband calls you too sensitive. That leaves you feeling like a stranger in the home you share with them.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: Betrayed by your own family, you may find that nothing feels like it matters right now. In the Yoga Vasishtha, young Rama asks what a kingdom or pleasures are to him, and who he really is. This questioning can sit with you as an honest doorway rather than a dead end, inviting you to look again at what remains when old loyalties fall away.
meaning: Young Rama speaks in his father's court after returning from travels. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask why he seems so low. Rama answers by questioning the value of kingship and pleasure. He asks who he is and what all this is for. He suggests that if the world is unreal, let it be unreal, and asks who truly owns anything and what anyone has gained. The text treats this honest naming of emptiness as the first step of inquiry, not a final answer. Your family broke something you counted on. That loss can make the work you do and the life you built feel hollow. Rama's question names that hollowness without rushing to fix it.

verse_text.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse_text.setting: Ashtavakra's 'special instruction' to Janaka on why striving and study do not bring peace.
verse_text.line: Enjoy, work or meditate all you like: your heart still longs for the place where wanting stops.
verse_text.translation: Wise one, enjoy, work or meditate as you will: your mind will still long for that state where every want has dropped away.

days.reading: Ashtavakra tells Janaka to enjoy, work, or meditate as he likes, yet his heart still longs for where wanting stops. You have tried doing everything right and still feel lost. The verse sees this restlessness not as a failure of your efforts, but as the mind pointing beyond every activity toward a place where every want has dropped away.

verse_text.speaker: Shaunaka
verse_text.setting: A wealthy householder comes formally to a teacher with one question.
verse_text.line: Shaunaka asked: what is the one thing which, once known, makes everything else make sense?
verse_text.translation: Shaunaka, the great householder, approached Angiras in the proper way and asked: 'Sir, what is that which, when known, makes all this known?'

days.reading: Shaunaka, a wealthy householder, formally approached the teacher Angiras and asked what single thing, once known, makes everything else make sense. You carry the weight of being betrayed by your own family while working through days that feel empty. This question names the ground beneath scattered pain: there is one reality behind the variety you face, and asking it with humility is where you stand.

verse_text.speaker: Angiras
verse_text.setting: The two birds, continued.
verse_text.line: The bird that eats grieves, lost in its helplessness. When it sees the calm one beside it, grief falls away.
verse_text.translation: On the same tree a person sits sunk, grieving, bewildered by his own helplessness. When he sees the other, the content lord, and his greatness, his sorrow leaves him.

days.reading: Angiras tells Shaunaka about two birds on one tree: one eats and grieves, lost in helplessness, until it sees the calm one beside it and his greatness, and then sorrow falls away. You feel lost after being betrayed by your own family, and right now the struggle seems to own you. Notice the part of you that can simply watch the pain without drowning in the story, and let that steadier view ease the weight today.

verse_text.speaker: Vasishtha
verse_text.setting: Vasishtha defines inquiry (vichara).
verse_text.line: Ask honestly: Who am I? How did I get caught in this? That questioning is inquiry.
verse_text.translation: 'Who am I? How did this trouble called worldly life come upon me?' Reflecting on this rightly is called inquiry.

days.reading: Vasishtha tells Rama to ask honestly, 'Who am I? How did I get caught in this?' This inquiry means calmly investigating who you really are and how this trouble came upon you. You could write these two questions on paper today and sit with them for a few minutes without forcing an answer.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Janaka and others reached fulfilment through action. Keep working, if only for the good of the world.
verse_text.translation: Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone. And looking to the welfare of the world, you too should act.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that wise figures like Janaka reached fulfilment through action, and even without personal need, one can act for the good of the world. You could direct one small task today toward someone else, letting their reliance on it give today a shape. This does not measure your worth, nor does it ask you to ignore the emptiness you carry.

story.title: Rama's lament: what is the point of all this?
story.summary: Asked to speak, Rama pours out what he has seen: wealth hardens people, life drips away like water off a leaf, ego and craving run us, the mind never fills, childhood, youth and old age each bring their own suffering, and time eats everything. He ends by saying only the company of good people gives him hope.
story.lesson: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.

days.reading: Rama tells the court that people are born to die and die to be born, and asks what this happiness is. After travelling, he lists everything he was told to want—wealth, ego, the body, time—and finds each unsteady. You, feeling lost after being betrayed by your own family, hear him lay his pain before the assembly and ask how to live without being crushed, rather than retreating into silence.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.
verse_text.line: Quiet, you're dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga.
verse_text.translation: Keep quiet and you are dumb; speak well and you are a babbler or a windbag; stay close and you are pushy; keep away and you lack confidence; be patient and you are a coward; refuse to put up with things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis.

reading: You trusted a friend with your business, and they stabbed you in the back. Bhartrihari tells the reader that when you serve someone powerful, staying quiet makes you dull, speaking up makes you a show-off, and being patient makes you weak. The verse shows that any choice can be twisted into a fault by the person in power. Today, this means your anger makes sense against a setup where every move is judged unfairly, not against your own actions.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks from his section on wicked people. He is describing the courtier who serves a master. No matter what the servant does, the master finds a fault. Stay silent and you are dull. Speak well and you are a babbler. Stay close and you are pushy. Keep away and you lack confidence. Be patient and you are weak. Refuse to endure and you are ill bred. Serving another is a duty so deep that even yogis cannot fathom it.

verse_text.speaker: the gopis
verse_text.setting: The women of Braj, after Krishna has left, on missing him.
verse_text.line: "Since he left, it has been monsoon in our eyes."
verse_text.translation: Night and day our eyes keep raining. Ever since Shyam went away, it is always the rainy season for us.

reading: Since he left, it has been monsoon in our eyes. The gopis say night and day their eyes keep raining, because Shyam went away. Your daughter’s silence has turned two years into a season that does not lift, and naming that weather is part of how you still hold her. You can let the rain be there.
meaning: The gopis, the cowherd women of Braj, speak these words to a friend after Krishna has gone. They tell her that since Shyam left their village, their eyes weep night and day without pause. The verse says their mourning has become a season rather than a single storm. Tears for someone you miss are allowed, and the longing itself is treated as a form of love. Your daughter's silence has turned two years into a season that does not lift, and naming that weather is part of how you still hold her. You can let the rain be there.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: You feel dismissed when you speak up and your parents side with your brother instead. In the Shanti Parva, Krishna says his own relatives' harsh words keep burning him day after day. Your hurt carries the same sting of words from those closest to you that refuse to cool.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after his own clan has split into feuds. He tells Narada that he gives his kin half of what he owns and bears their harsh words, yet those words grind his heart like a fire-stick being churned. The verse proposes that in family conflict the only effective weapon is not force but gentleness, patience and respect. Your hurt carries the same sting of words from those closest to you that refuse to cool.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)

verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: You carry the sting of words that cut in front of others. Krishna speaks of his own heart being churned like a fire-stick by the harsh words of relatives, burning day after day. That same lingering heat can sit with you now, without asking you to carry it forever.
meaning: Krishna tells the sage Narada that his heart is churned like a fire-stick by the harsh words of his relatives. He bears their cruelty while doing their work, yet the words grind his heart and keep burning him day after day. The point is that in family feuds, gentleness, patience and respect are the only weapons that work. Your brother's words at the wedding still burn because they were spoken in front of others. The heat you feel now is the same lingering fire Krishna describes.

verse_text.translation: Night and day our eyes keep raining. Ever since Shyam went away, it is always the rainy season for us.

reading: Since he left, it has been monsoon in our eyes. You are carrying a first real breakup after being together all through high school, and now the days can feel like a season that does not lift. This verse names that kind of missing as its own form of love, not an event to fix. Let your eyes keep raining for now.
meaning: The women of Braj speak these lines after Krishna has gone away. They tell a friend that night and day their eyes keep raining. Ever since Shyam left, it is always the rainy season for them. The verse proposes that tears for someone you miss are allowed. The loss is so total that weeping becomes a season rather than a single event. Your missing her is not a problem to solve. It is a form of love that has its own weather, and that is allowed.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse_text.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

reading: You are in a house that feels empty after twenty years of marriage. Ram tells Sita that speaking of pain lightens it a little, yet no one else can know this ache; only the heart knows the love it misses. That private ache is real, and naming it here, in this quiet room, is a small relief you can hold today.
meaning: Ram sends this message to Sita through Hanuman. She is held captive by Ravana in the grove, and hope has nearly left her. Hanuman has just told her Ram's story and dropped Ram's ring into her hands. Ram says that speaking of pain lightens it a little. But he asks whom he can tell, because no one else knows this ache. Only his own heart knows the truth of the love between them.

Perhaps today you can notice the weight in your own chest, and let that private knowing sit with you without trying to fix it.

After nine years in the same bed, you carry a silence that no argument broke. The verse holds that ache as real and private, not as your failure.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: Your mind keeps searching those last years for the moment love slipped away, yet it feels as hard to hold as the wind. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. Today, your thoughts may race through the same dinner conversation again and again, not because you are failing, but because a mind this strong simply does not settle on command. You can notice the loop without forcing it to stop.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes the steady evenness of the highest yogi. Arjuna objects that such control is impossible because the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He says it is as hard to hold as the wind. The verse takes this complaint seriously and names the mind's force. It proposes that the mind is hard to steady, yet practice and letting go can train it. Your mind keeps searching those last years for the moment love slipped away, yet it feels as hard to hold as the wind. That searching is not a failure on your part.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: You are 8000 miles from your mom in Indore while she stays alone. Krishna, far from home, tells his mother that since he left, no one has called him by his pet name, and he has missed his morning food and evening warm milk. In your distance today, the verse speaks of missing the ordinary tenderness of home—a familiar name, a simple meal—rather than grand gestures. You might hold her pet name for her in your thoughts, and remember the warmth of that evening milk she once shared.
meaning: Krishna sends a message through to his foster mother Yashoda. He tells her to stay well and that the two brothers will come in four or five days. He adds that since the day he left her, no one has called him by his pet name Kanhaiya, and he has not had his morning breakfast or evening warm milk. Your distance from Indore carries the same ordinary tenderness. The verse holds that missing home is love, not only your longing but hers too.

verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You are in your first job in another state, and your papa has just retired to be home alone with mumma while your mind races. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and as hard to hold as the wind. When you lie awake wondering if they are okay, you are holding something as elusive as air. The wind does not stay still in your hands, and that restless motion is simply what the mind is doing right now.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes the steady yogi who feels all beings as his own. Arjuna objects that such evenness cannot last. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna answers that practice and letting go can train it. Your mind is doing exactly what Arjuna named. The worry about your parents is real, but the racing itself is just the mind moving like air.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You placed your father in a care home and now live each day wrapped in guilt. Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against their will, as if pushed by force. This verse meets your sorrow by naming the question itself as real and worthy, without judging the care you chose.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against their own will, as if pushed by force. Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger, and this desire is the enemy that clouds wisdom like smoke over fire. He tells Arjuna to master it by seeing it clearly. Your guilt carries the same shape Arjuna names. You did not choose this care home lightly, and the verse lets you ask why the wrong feels forced upon you without calling you wicked.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: You are far from your mum on her birthday, cutting a cake over a screen. Krishna, now far from home in Mathura, tells his mother Yashoda that since he left, no one has called him by his pet name, Kanhaiya, and he has missed his morning breakfast and evening warm milk. In your distance today, the verse names what only home gives: not grand gestures, but being known by your home name and being fed. That ordinary tenderness still exists on the other side of the call.
meaning: Krishna sends a message to his foster mother Yashoda through. He is in Mathura, far. He tells her to stay well and that he and his brother will return in four or five days. He adds that since the day he left, no one has called him by his pet name Kanhaiya. He has also missed his morning breakfast and his evening warm milk. The distance you feel today is the same love that moves across it. What you miss is not a grand reunion but the small recognitions only home gives.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: Your sixteen-year-old son stays up all night on his phone and shuts the door when you speak. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. You do not have to steady it by force tonight; simply noticing how hard it is to hold can be enough, like standing still while the wind moves.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes the highest yogi who feels all beings' joy and pain as his own. Arjuna objects that such steady evenness cannot last because the mind is too restless. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and as hard to hold as the wind. The verse proposes that the mind is difficult to steady, yet practice and letting go can train it. Your son's closed door and his late nights with the phone show a mind that will not settle. The verse names that restlessness as real, not your failure, and points toward patient practice rather than force.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You are carrying school runs, swim class, homework, and work calls with no time to breathe as a dad. The Yoga Vasishtha describes a mind caught on endless waves of tasks—'this I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do'—fainting in a net of reckonings. Your restlessness today mirrors that bird of the mind, swept along without a moment's rest. You might notice the to-do loop running in the background, and step back from it just enough to feel the pause between one duty and the next.
meaning: Bhasa speaks to his old friend Vilasa, two men who grew up together in a forest hermitage and later spent years apart in hard austerities. When they meet again as old men, Vilasa asks if Bhasa has found peace. Bhasa answers that he has not. He says the mind is carried on endless waves of tasks. It reckons what is done, what is doing, and what must still be done. Caught in this net of reckonings, the bird of the mind faints and finds no rest. Your days of school runs, swim class, homework and work calls echo that endless wave. The restlessness you feel is the mind fainting in its own net of duties.

verse_text.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse_text.setting: Ashtavakra's 'special instruction' to Janaka on why striving and study do not bring peace.
verse_text.line: Everyone suffers from constant straining, and no one notices. Seeing this alone brings peace.
verse_text.translation: Everyone is miserable from straining after things, and no one realises it. By this single teaching the fortunate one finds peace.

days.reading: Ashtavakra tells Janaka that everyone suffers from constant straining, yet no one notices it. The verse sees this misery coming from the anxious grip of desire-driven striving that rides on top of ordinary effort. You carry a quiet worry about your daughter, and today the text simply points to the extra layer of strain layered over your care, inviting you to notice it without judging the work itself.

verse_text.speaker: Seer
verse_text.setting: The second birth: raising a child.
verse_text.line: Caring for your child, you care for yourself. Through them you are born a second time.
verse_text.translation: When he cares for the child from birth onward, he is caring for himself, for the continuation of these worlds; that is how they continue. That is his second birth.

days.reading: The Aitareya Upanishad says that when you care for your child from birth onward, you are caring for yourself, because that is your second birth. In the midst of your overthinking, this means the daily nurturing you give your daughter is also tending to your own continuation. Let that ground hold you today.

verse_text.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse_text.speaker: Yudhishthira
verse_text.setting: In exile, Draupadi urges Yudhishthira to answer injustice with force; he argues for forgiveness.
verse_text.line: Don't answer anger with anger. The one who stays calm protects both people, and heals both.
verse_text.translation: One who does not get angry back at an angry person saves both himself and the other from great danger. He becomes the healer of both.

days.reading: Yudhishthira tells Draupadi not to answer anger with anger. The one who stays calm protects both people and heals both. In the middle of your overthinking, you can choose to be that steady presence, letting your daughter’s quiet world and your own breath slow down without forcing anything.

verse_text.speaker: Seer
verse_text.setting: The Aitareya on the three births of a person, beginning with pregnancy.
verse_text.line: She who nourishes the child must herself be nourished.
verse_text.translation: It becomes one with the woman, like a part of her own body, so it does not harm her. She nourishes this self of his that has come into her. She who nourishes must herself be nourished. The woman carries the child; the father cares for the child from birth onward.

days.reading: The Aitareya Upanishad says that she who nourishes the child must herself be nourished. Since your daughter is still finding her voice, you carry so much worry. You could ask one person today to take over her bedtime so you can eat a proper meal in peace.

verse_text.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse_text.setting: 'The Ideal of a Universal Religion', America, on how anyone grows.
verse_text.line: Your duty is to afford opportunities and to remove obstacles.
verse_text.translation: Do you think you can teach even a child? You cannot. The child teaches himself. Your duty is to afford opportunities and to remove obstacles. A plant grows. Do you make the plant grow? Your duty is to put a hedge round it and see that no animal eats up the plant, and there your duty ends.

days.reading: Swami Vivekananda says a plant grows on its own; your duty is only to put a hedge around it and keep animals away. You could clear one small obstacle today and then step back, letting your daughter find her own way to speak. The hedge is your steady care, not forcing a word from her.

story.title: A poor widow's small son is afraid to walk home through the woods
story.summary: Gopala's mother is a widow, very poor, who has toiled at her spinning wheel for months to buy his school things. One winter afternoon he tells her he is afraid to walk home alone through the dark woods; other boys have someone to fetch them. 'Never before had she felt her widowhood, her loneliness, her poverty so bitter.'
story.lesson: A parent's faith, passed to a child, makes the child unafraid; love and faith, more than learning, bring the Lord near.

days.reading: Swami Vivekananda retold a devotional tale of a poor widow whose son Gopala fears walking home through dark woods. When her loneliness feels bitter, she remembers that the Lord carries what dependent ones need, and tells her boy to call his brother Gopala, who tends cattle there. Your worry about your daughter not yet speaking meets this mother’s dark moment: faith passed to a child can quiet fear, even when the path ahead looks lonely.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Rama describes his restless mind to the sages.
verse_text.line: The mind pounces on a task like a bird on food, then drops it like a bored child's toy.
verse_text.translation: The mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy.

reading: You have been saying 'starting the gym on monday' since January. Rama tells the sages that the mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, then loses interest like a child with a toy. This pattern of beginning and dropping is an ordinary feature of the untrained mind, not a flaw in you. When you notice the mind letting go, you can simply return to the weights in front of you.
meaning: Rama speaks to the sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha after they ask why he has grown so withdrawn. He describes what he has observed about the world and about his own thinking. He says the mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy. He is naming the problem honestly. He is not yet offering the answer. You have been telling yourself you will start the gym on Monday since January. This verse names that pattern without calling it a flaw in you.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You have wanted to write a book for ten years without finishing a single chapter, and now nothing feels like it matters. Young Rama asks what a kingdom or pleasure is to him, and who he really is. This questioning of everything he has can be the healthy start of a real inquiry for you today, opening the path toward what truly matters.
meaning: Young Rama sits in his father's court after returning from his travels. The sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask him why he looks so low. Rama answers by questioning the worth of his kingdom and his pleasures. He asks who he is and what all this is for. He suggests that if the world is unreal, let it be unreal, and asks whose it truly is and what anyone has gained. The text treats this honest naming of emptiness as the first step of inquiry, not as a final answer. Your ten year wish to write a book has stayed unwritten, and now the weight of that gap makes the world feel flat.

verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: Arjuna asks this, and many of us ask it too: what pushes a person to do wrong, even unwillingly, as if forced? If you're carrying something you did, you've probably asked it at night. The Gita treats the question as worth a full answer.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong against his will, as if pushed by force. Krishna answers that unfulfilled desire turns into anger, and this anger clouds wisdom like smoke over fire. The verse proposes that one must see this desire clearly and master it, rather than blaming an outside force. You feel trapped by tasks you never started, and the guilt is heavy because you know the time was there. The verse suggests the push comes from inside, not from a lack of hours.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Rama describes his restless mind to the sages.
verse_text.line: The mind pounces on a task like a bird on food, then drops it like a bored child's toy.
verse_text.translation: The mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy.

reading: Your mind keeps landing on tasks like a bird on food, then dropping them like a bored child's toy. The Yoga Vasishtha names this restlessness honestly: the untrained mind grabs what attracts it and lets it go almost at once. This pattern is an ordinary feature of the mind, not a personal defect. When you sit down to work today, notice the swoop and the drop without blaming yourself for either.
meaning: Rama speaks to the sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha after they ask why he has grown so withdrawn. He is describing his own restless mind. He says the mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy. He is naming a problem honestly. The verse proposes that seeing this empty grabbing and dropping clearly is the first step. It does not yet offer the answer. You told me you feel stuck in procrastination. This verse names that same restless pattern without calling it a flaw in you. It simply shows the mind grabbing and letting go, and that naming it is where clarity begins.

When you notice a project stalling today, you can simply name the drop without blaming yourself, and let the next small step be enough.

The mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy. He is naming a restless habit, not offering a cure. Your half finished projects sit in the same restless current Rama describes. The pattern is older than your will.

reading: After the kids sleep, you plan to work on your online shop but find yourself not starting. Rama tells the sages that the mind pounces on a task like a bird on food, then drops it like a bored child's toy. This restless habit is simply how an untrained mind behaves, not a flaw in you. Tonight, you might simply place one small item for sale beside the bed, letting the work begin without pressure.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You feel restless, caught between wanting to begin today and watching the day slip away. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go; they do not last, so bear them patiently. When you sit down to study, notice that this restlessness, like the weather, has a beginning and an end.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These feelings come and go. They do not last. Arjuna must bear them patiently. The teaching is that the true self outlasts every loss and every passing pain. Your restlessness comes and goes too. It is not the whole of your study life, and it does not have to decide your next move today.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: Arjuna asks this, and many of us ask it too: what pushes a person to do wrong, even unwillingly, as if forced? If you're carrying something you did, you've probably asked it at night. The Gita treats the question as worth a full answer.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against their own will, as if pushed by some outside force. Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger, and this desire is the enemy that clouds a person's wisdom like smoke over a fire. The verse proposes that you can master this force once you see it clearly for what it is.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'The Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures'.
verse_text.line: The moth doesn't know the flame burns. We know, and still we don't let go.
verse_text.translation: Let the moth fall into the blazing flame not knowing that it burns; let the fish swallow the bait not knowing the hook. But we, knowing full well, still do not let go of desires tangled in a net of dangers. Ah, how deep is the power of delusion!

reading: You notice the last watch already feels old. Bhartrihari says the moth knows the flame burns, yet still flies in; we see the danger and still do not let go. That restlessness you feel is the net of dangers he names, not a flaw in you. Today, when the next car catches your eye, let that knowing pause sit with you before you reach.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks from his Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures. He addresses the reader directly. He sets up the moth and the fish. Both creatures fall into ruin without knowing the danger. Then he turns to us. We know the flame burns and the hook waits. Yet we still clutch at desires that tangle us in a net of harm. He asks how deep the power of delusion runs when knowledge does not free us. You already own the last watch and it feels stale. Bhartrihari names the same trap you are in, where knowing the cost does not loosen the grip.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You feel controlled by sale notifications and find your closet full of tagged items. Krishna tells Arjuna that contact of the senses with objects brings heat and cold, pleasure and pain that come and go, and asks us to bear them patiently. These urges to buy and the discomfort behind them are contacts that touch you and then move on. You can simply notice the notification arrive and pass, without letting it steer what stays in your closet.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that contact between the senses and their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These feelings come and go and do not last. He asks Arjuna to bear them patiently. The urge to buy and the restlessness behind it are contacts that touch you and then move on. You do not have to let them steer what stays in your closet.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'The Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures'.
verse_text.line: The moth doesn't know the flame burns. We know, and still we don't let go.
verse_text.translation: Let the moth fall into the blazing flame not knowing that it burns; let the fish swallow the bait not knowing the hook. But we, knowing full well, still do not let go of desires tangled in a net of dangers. Ah, how deep is the power of delusion!

reading: You mentioned reels pulling you past 2 AM. Bhartrihari writes that the moth knows the flame burns, yet still does not let go. You see the cost, and still the scroll keeps you there. The verse names that pull as deep delusion, not a private failing. Tonight, when the phone lights up, let the screen stay dark for one minute before you touch it.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks this from the Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures. He looks at creatures driven by instinct. The moth flies into the flame without knowing it burns. The fish swallows the bait without knowing the hook waits. But humans see the danger clearly. We still grip desires that trap us in a net of harm. He calls this deep delusion. We cling even though we know the cost. You already see the cost of those late reels. The verse names that pull as a shared human pattern, not a private failing on your part.

verse_text.speaker: Nidagha
verse_text.setting: Nidagha on craving.
verse_text.line: Every good quality I take up, craving gnaws through, like a mouse chewing a string.
verse_text.translation: Whatever good quality I take refuge in, great sage, craving cuts it away, as a mouse gnaws through a string.

reading: You notice that every good resolve you make gets quietly undone, much like a mouse gnawing through a string. The Maha Upanishad has Ribhu say that whatever good quality you take up, craving cuts it away. Today, that next purchase might feel like a celebration, yet the wanting behind it keeps fraying what you are trying to build. You could simply notice the craving itself, without judging the flat savings.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'The Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures'.
verse_text.line: The moth doesn't know the flame burns. We know, and still we don't let go.

meaning: Bhartrihari speaks this from the section that mocks our failure to give up pleasures. He looks at the moth and the fish. The moth flies into the flame without knowing it burns. The fish swallows the bait without knowing the hook waits. But we know the danger. We see the net of troubles around our cravings. And still we do not let go. The verse says we should release these desires before force removes them. It also says we must stop calling that forced removal relief or happiness. You named a greed that still pulls at you even now. The verse shows that knowing the cost is not the same as stepping back.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'The Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures'.
verse_text.line: The moth doesn't know the flame burns. We know, and still we don't let go.

meaning: Bhartrihari speaks this from the section that mocks our failure to give up pleasures. He sets the moth and the fish beside us. The moth flies into the flame without knowing it burns. The fish swallows the bait without knowing the hook waits. We are different. We see the danger clearly. We know the flame will hurt us. We know the hook will catch us. Still we do not let go. We hold on to desires that are tangled in a net of dangers. The poet asks how deep this power of delusion runs. You know the sweetness is not what you need, yet your hand reaches for it anyway.

verse_text.speaker: Indra, disguised as a jackal
verse_text.setting: The jackal tells Kashyapa that getting more will not cure his discontent.
verse_text.line: Getting what you want doesn't satisfy. Craving grows like a fire fed with more wood.
verse_text.translation: There is no satisfaction in getting what you want. Craving is not put out by water; it only blazes up more, like a fire fed with fuel.

days.reading: The jackal tells Kashyapa that getting what you want does not satisfy. Craving is not put out by water; it only blazes up more, like a fire fed with fuel. You reach for one more sweet, then another, yet the hunger only grows. Notice the flame before you add to it today.

verse_text.speaker: Yama
verse_text.setting: Nachiketa has refused wealth and long life; Yama begins teaching.
verse_text.line: The good and the pleasant both knock. The wise choose the good; the foolish grab the pleasant.
verse_text.translation: The good and the pleasant both come to a person. The wise one examines them and tells them apart. The wise chooses the good over the pleasant; the dull chooses the pleasant, for getting and keeping.

days.reading: Yama tells Nachiketa that the good and the pleasant both knock at the door. The wise examine and separate them, choosing the good, while the careless grab the pleasant for getting and keeping. You feel restless as sweets call to you, yet today you can simply pause and ask whether what you want is good for you or just pleasant right now.

verse_text.speaker: Manki
verse_text.setting: Manki, after his last savings are lost in a freak accident, speaks to his own desire.
verse_text.line: Desire, I know your root: my own imagining. I'll stop feeding you, and you'll be gone.
verse_text.translation: Desire, I know your root: you are born of my own imagining. I will not imagine you any more, and you will be gone, root and all.

days.reading: Manki tells his own desire, 'I know your root: you are born of my own imagining. I will stop imagining you, and you will vanish.' You keep promising yourself you will stop, yet the wanting returns. Today’s job is to give you ground to stand on: notice the moment you start picturing what you want, and let that image go. When you stop feeding the picture, the restless pull loses its hold.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Like a tortoise pulling in its limbs, draw your senses back from what pulls at them.
verse_text.translation: When, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs on every side, a person withdraws the senses from their objects, his wisdom is firmly set.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to draw the senses back from their objects like a tortoise pulling in its limbs. You could try one small move today: when the pull toward something sweet or a screen spikes, close the tab or step back. Notice the pull fade, then let your hand rest.

verse_text.speaker: Vasishtha
verse_text.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
verse_text.line: When your mind drifts to harmful things, steer it back to good ones. That's the whole teaching.
verse_text.translation: When the mind has sunk into bad things, bring it down into good ones with effort. That is the summary of all the scriptures.

days.reading: Vasishtha tells Rama: when the mind sinks into harmful things, steer it back to good ones with effort. You could try this today by choosing one small, steady task the moment you notice your attention drifting toward what you crave. This is not about forcing away restlessness, but gently placing your mind somewhere else.

story.title: Manki's song: desire, I know your root
story.summary: Manki spends all he has on a pair of oxen; both are killed in an accident. In his despair he sees through desire: it is born of his own imagining, and he resolves to forgive insults and stop feeding it. Bhishma adds Janaka's verse on owning nothing.
story.lesson: Desire grows from what we imagine. Stop feeding it, and it fades.

days.reading: Manki loses his last money when a camel bolts with the two young bulls he bought, leaving him to watch them dangle and die. Out of weariness, he turns on desire itself, saying it is born of his own imagining and that he will stop imagining it so it vanishes at the root. Like your daily cycle of promising and breaking your resolve around the sweet, his loss did not end in blame but in cutting the root of wanting.

verse_text.speaker: Nidagha
verse_text.setting: Nidagha on craving.
verse_text.line: Every good quality I take up, craving gnaws through, like a mouse chewing a string.
verse_text.translation: Whatever good quality I take refuge in, great sage, craving cuts it away, as a mouse gnaws through a string.

reading: You feel restless, always wanting more. The Maha Upanishad has Nidagha say that whatever good quality he takes up, craving gnaws through it like a mouse chewing a string. This speaks to you today as a quiet pattern that can fray your efforts from within, not a flaw in your character. Notice where that background wanting nibbles, and place one small barrier between you and the next pull.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You order things online every week and the house fills up, yet the emptiness stays. Young Rama asks what a kingdom or pleasure means to him, and who he really is. This same questioning of everything gathered can meet you exactly where you are, opening a real inquiry into what matters beyond the next delivery.
meaning: Young Rama has just returned from travels. He sits in his father's court. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask why he seems so low. Rama answers by asking what a kingdom or pleasure means to him. He asks who he is and what all this gathered wealth is for. He says if it is unreal, let it be unreal. He asks whose it is and what anyone has gained. The text treats this honest naming of emptiness as the first step of inquiry, not as a final answer.

verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You asked what drives a person to do wrong even against their will, as if pushed by force. Arjuna voices this exact struggle: doing the thing you do not want, yet finding yourself pulled back in. The Gita takes that question seriously, naming it as a real conflict rather than a personal failure. When the next match calls after 4 a.m., you can notice the pull without letting it define you.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against his own will, as if forced by an outside power. Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger, and this desire is the true enemy that clouds a person's wisdom like smoke over a fire. The verse proposes that a person can master this force by seeing it clearly for what it is.

verse_text.speaker: Vibhishan
verse_text.setting: Vibhishan, Ravana's good-hearted brother, describes his life in Ravana's court.
verse_text.line: I live here like the tongue among the teeth.
verse_text.translation: Son of the wind, hear how I live: like the poor tongue among the teeth. Friend, knowing me to be without support, will the Lord of the Sun dynasty ever show me grace?

reading: It sounds like home doesn't feel safe right now.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You have a good salary, a nice flat, and a healthy family, yet inside it all feels flat, and you wonder if this is it. Young Rama asks what a kingdom or pleasure is to him, who he really is, and what all this is for. That questioning of everything you have built can meet the flatness you feel today, pointing toward the real question of who you are beyond the roles that look successful.
meaning: Young Rama has just returned from his travels. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask why he looks so low. Rama answers that nothing interests him anymore. He asks what kingship or pleasure means to him, who he really is, and what all this is for. He suggests that if the world is unreal, let it be unreal, and asks who truly owns anything and what anyone has gained. The text treats this honest naming of emptiness as the first step of inquiry, not as a final answer. Your good salary, your nice flat, and your healthy family sit beside a flatness you cannot shake. Rama's question meets that exact feeling and points toward who you are beyond the roles that look successful.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: The narrator Sanjaya speaks these words. He describes the greatest archer of his time putting down his bow and sitting in the chariot, his mind sunk in sorrow. The Gita begins with someone who can't go on, and it stays with him for seventeen more chapters.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You asked what the point of padhai, naukri, shaadi, bachche is when nothing feels like it matters. Young Rama asks the same in his father's court: what is kingship or pleasure to me, who am I, and what is all this for? This questioning is not a dead end but the healthy start of inquiry, opening space to explore what actually matters to you right now.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: Your days blur together and nothing feels meaningful anymore. Young Rama asks, what is a kingdom or pleasure to me, who am I, and what is all this for? When everything you do feels hollow, that emptiness can open a real question about what matters, pointing toward who you are beneath the routine. Let this quiet wondering sit with you today as you move through your next ordinary task.
meaning: Young Rama returns from his travels and sits in his father's court. The sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask him why he looks so low. Rama answers that he has seen how wealth hardens people and how life slips away. He asks what a kingdom or pleasure means to him, who he really is, and what all this is for. If the world is unreal, let it be unreal. The text treats this honest naming of emptiness as the first step of inquiry, not as a final answer. When your days blur together and nothing feels meaningful, that hollow feeling is not a failure. It is the same honest question Rama asks, the start of looking deeper rather than a sign that something is broken in you.

verse_text.speaker: Narada
verse_text.setting: Narada, master of every science, comes to Sanatkumara.
verse_text.line: I have learned so much, yet I am sad. I know words, not myself. Help me cross this sorrow.
verse_text.translation: 'Sir, I know only the texts; I do not know the self. I have heard from people like you that one who knows the self crosses beyond sorrow. I am in sorrow, sir. Please take me across.' He said to him: 'Whatever you have studied is only name.'

reading: After twenty years abroad earning for your family and building a settled life back home, you now sit in your room and feel like an empty box. Narada, who had mastered every science, admitted to Sanatkumara, "I know words, not myself," and asked simply to be taken across his sorrow. Your own learning and doing can meet the same honest limit today, opening space to ask what lies beyond what you have accomplished.
meaning: Narada, a master of every science of his day, comes to Sanatkumara and admits that despite his vast learning he remains sad. He tells Sanatkumara that he knows words and texts but not the self. Sanatkumara replies that whatever Narada has studied is only name. The verse proposes that success and learning do not cure sadness, and only the infinite does.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: Every day the same question comes: why am I doing all this? Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go, and do not last; bear them patiently. You do not have to carry the weight of this daily question as a permanent truth. Notice how this pressure, too, arrives and passes like weather, and let your feet rest in the moment before the next demand.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after Arjuna has voiced his grief over the coming battle. Krishna reminds him that the true Self is never born and never dies.
