reading: You are writing your dissertation, putting in 500 words a day no matter what. Swami Vivekananda wrote that each work has to pass through stages of ridicule, opposition, and then acceptance, and that anyone who thinks ahead of their time is sure to be misunderstood. Your daily resolve already carries you forward; when doubt or pushback appears, see it as a stage to move through, and keep your own conduct steady as you continue.
meaning: Swami Vivekananda wrote this from America on the ninth of July eighteen ninety five. He sent it, the Maharaja of Khetri, his patron and close friend. Some clergy in America were opposing his work. Vivekananda told the Maharaja that every new work moves through three stages. First comes ridicule, then opposition, and finally acceptance. He added that anyone who thinks ahead of their time will be misunderstood. The verse proposes that resistance is a normal stage, not a final verdict on the work itself. Your dissertation is new work, and the daily grind already meets its own quiet resistance. What you feel now is the weight of that middle stage.

verse_text.speaker: Savitri
verse_text.setting: Knowing her husband will die in three days, Savitri takes a hard three-night vow; her father-in-law worries.
verse_text.line: I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end.
verse_text.translation: Don't be distressed, father. I will see this vow through. It was begun with determination, and determination is what carries it to the end.

reading: You are holding to discipline every day. Savitri tells her father-in-law that her vow was begun with determination, and that same determination carries it to the end. Let that same steadiness carry your resolve forward today, one day at a time.
meaning: Savitri speaks to her blind father-in-law Dyumatsena. She knows her husband Satyavan will die in three days. She has begun a severe three-night vow without food. Dyumatsena worries at its harshness. Savitri tells him not to grieve. She says she started this vow with determination. That same determination is what carries it to the end. You are holding to discipline every day. Savitri's steadiness mirrors the resolve you already carry.

verse_text.speaker: Nidagha
verse_text.setting: Nidagha on craving.
verse_text.line: Every good quality I take up, craving gnaws through, like a mouse chewing a string.
verse_text.translation: Whatever good quality I take refuge in, great sage, craving cuts it away, as a mouse gnaws through a string.

reading: You feel restless even after losing 15 kg and committing to keep it off, as the old habits keep calling. The Maha Upanishad says that whatever good quality we take up, craving gnaws through it, like a mouse chewing a string. This quiet nibbling may be what frays your resolve today, not a lack in you. You might notice the craving itself when the old habits call, and place one small practical barrier between you and the bait.
meaning: Nidagha speaks to his teacher Ribhu, the great sage, after returning from a pilgrimage filled with disillusionment. He laments that life slips away and the mind runs wild like a stray dog. In this moment he names a deeper trouble. Whatever good quality he takes up as a refuge, craving cuts it away. It acts exactly like a mouse gnawing through a string.

verse_text.speaker: Savitri
verse_text.setting: Knowing her husband will die in three days, Savitri takes a hard three-night vow; her father-in-law worries.
verse_text.line: I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end.
verse_text.translation: Don't be distressed, father. I will see this vow through. It was begun with determination, and determination is what carries it to the end.

reading: You promised your doctor you would walk every evening and stop the sweets, and you are holding to it. Savitri tells her father-in-law, I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end: I will see this vow through. Your own steady resolve is what began this change and what will carry it forward. Let that same determination guide your steps this evening.
meaning: Savitri speaks to her blind father-in-law Dyumatsena. He is distressed because she has begun a severe three-night vow while knowing her husband Satyavan will die soon. She tells him not to grieve. She began the observance with firm resolve, and that same resolve is what will carry it to completion. She will see the vow through to the end. You began this change with your own resolve, and that same steadiness is what will see you through the evenings ahead.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You have never read the Gita properly and want to know what it is actually about. Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people worship the divine: those in distress, those seeking wealth, those seeking knowledge, and the wise. Your curiosity places you among the seekers of knowledge, and the Gita welcomes you exactly as you are. You can open the text now, without any prior mastery, and meet it as your starting point.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He says all four kinds of good people worship him. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. It does not shut out those who come because they are hurting or in need. You have never read the Gita properly and want to know what it is actually about. Your curiosity places you among those seeking knowledge, and the text welcomes you exactly as you are.

meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of people with good merit who do. Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas. verse_text.speaker: Narada
verse_text.setting: Narada, master of every science, comes to Sanatkumara.
verse_text.line: I have learned so much, yet I am sad. I know words, not myself. Help me cross this sorrow.
verse_text.translation: 'Sir, I know only the texts; I do not know the self. I have heard from people like you that one who knows the self crosses beyond sorrow. I am in sorrow, sir. Please take me across.' He said to him: 'Whatever you have studied is only name.'

reading: You are a second generation kid trying to reconnect with your roots, and the Gita feels like the obvious first step. Narada tells Sanatkumara that he has mastered every science yet remains sad, because he knows words but not the self. Your learning and effort so far may still leave you with this same gap, and naming that honestly to someone wiser is the real beginning of the path.
meaning: Narada, who has mastered every science of his day, comes to Sanatkumara and admits he is unhappy. He knows words, not himself. Sanatkumara tells him that whatever he has studied is only name. The verse proposes that success and learning do not cure sadness, and only the infinite does. Your effort to reconnect with your roots through the Gita may still leave you with this same gap between knowing texts and knowing yourself, and naming that honestly is the real beginning.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You asked what the Gita says dharma is. Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people worship him: those in distress, those seeking knowledge, those in need, and the wise. Your curiosity places you among those welcome at the door. The text names you as one who comes seeking understanding, not as someone who must first suffer or want something else.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that deluded people do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. These are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He says all four worship him. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. It does not demand a single motive. Your question about dharma places you among those who come seeking understanding. The text names you as one who comes curious, not as someone who must first suffer or want something else.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain, which come and go and do not last. You are feeling anxious while studying. This verse speaks to that by showing these sensations naturally begin and end, so you can bear them without letting panic take over. Notice one tight feeling in your body right now, and let it be just a passing weather.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield after Arjuna has laid down his weapons in grief. Arjuna is mourning the elders he must fight. Krishna tells him that sense contact with the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These arrive and depart and do not last. He asks Arjuna to bear them patiently. Your anxiety while studying is a sense contact that has a beginning and an end. It is not the whole of you.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You feel caught in a restless mind. Krishna hears Arjuna say the mind is turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. This verse names that struggle plainly, showing that an unsettled mind is a real experience today. The wind itself is named here, so you can notice one breath moving without forcing it to stop.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes the highest yogi. Arjuna objects that such steady evenness cannot last. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. It is as hard to hold as the wind. The verse proposes that the mind is difficult to steady, yet practice and letting go can train it. You are living with a mind that will not settle, and this verse names that exact restlessness without calling you careless.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You feel empty. The Yoga Vasishtha describes Rama losing his spark for jokes, pleasures, and work, falling into silence. That quiet withdrawal is noticed and taken seriously by those around him, who bring help rather than scolding. You do not have to carry this alone; letting someone close see this silence and reach out to you is a step worth taking today.
meaning: Dasharatha sends his servant to find out why Rama has changed since his pilgrimage. The servant reports that the prince no longer laughs at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work. He just keeps silent. The text treats this quiet withdrawal as a serious state that calls for care and conversation rather than scolding. You are carrying a silence that has swallowed your usual spark. The text shows that such quiet withdrawal is noticed and taken seriously by those around you, who can bring help if you let them see it.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Rama describes his restless mind to the sages.
verse_text.line: The mind pounces on a task like a bird on food, then drops it like a bored child's toy.
verse_text.translation: The mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy.

reading: You feel stuck and can't get started. Rama tells the sages that the mind swoops onto a task like a bird onto meat, then drops it a moment later like a bored child's toy. This pattern of starting and abandoning is simply how an untrained mind behaves, not a flaw in you. When you sit down to work today, notice if the mind has already hopped onto something else; simply naming that swoop is a gentle first step.
meaning: Rama speaks to the sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha after they ask why he has grown so withdrawn. He describes what he has observed about the world and about his own mind. He says the mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy. He is naming a restless pattern honestly. He is asking what the point of it all is, not offering a solution. You are facing a workday where nothing feels worth starting. Rama names this same swooping and dropping as the way an untrained mind behaves, not a flaw in your character.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You carry a heavy sense of guilt as you raise your kids. In the Gita, Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against their will, as if pushed by some force. This verse meets your struggle with honesty, naming the gap between what you want and what you did. You might rest in the simple truth that this question itself is real, and today you can simply notice where that force shows up in your own life.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even when they do not want to, as if pushed by some outside force. Krishna answers that an unmet desire turns into anger, and this desire is the enemy that clouds a person's wisdom like smoke hides a fire. He tells Arjuna to master this force rather than let it rule him. You feel guilty about past mistakes while raising your children. The verse meets that guilt by naming the gap between what you wanted and what you did, without calling you wicked.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: You feel hurt. Krishna says the deepest sorrow is not the loss itself, but that the one he loved did not face him and tell him directly. When someone close wounds you, the sting may come less from what happened and more from the silence or distance around it. You can sit with that specific ache of being kept in the dark, without forcing it into anything else.
meaning: Ram has just agreed to leave for the forest for fourteen years. Kaikeyi has told him that Bharata will be crowned instead. Ram accepts the exile without anger. Yet one thing still burns in him. He tells Kaikeyi that his deepest pain is not the news of the coronation. It is that his father did not come to him and tell him this himself. The wound you carry may be less about what happened and more about who chose not to face you with it.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: You carry a hurt that outlasts the loss itself. Ram says only one sorrow still burns his heart: that the king did not face him and tell him directly. When someone close wounds you by avoiding that hard conversation, naming the precise gap between what happened and how it reached you can begin to bear it.
meaning: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile without anger. Kaikeyi has told him that he must leave and that Bharata will be crowned. Ram agrees at once. Yet one thing still burns his heart. He says only one sorrow remains. The king did not tell him himself about Bharata's coronation. The verse proposes that a person can accept a loss. What wounds them is that the one they love did not face them and speak directly.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You feel lost right now. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed by grief to go on. This verse names the moment of laying everything down when you cannot move forward. The story does not end there; the next verses show him asking for help and finding a way ahead. You too can set down what you are carrying today and reach out for the next step.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. He reports that Arjuna has just spoken of his grief and fear. Arjuna then puts down his bow and arrows. He sits in his chariot, his mind overwhelmed by sorrow, too frozen to continue. This is the state you are in now, where the weight of things has stopped you in your tracks. The teaching begins here, with the freeze, not after it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You feel lonely right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever sees him everywhere and everything in him is never lost to him, nor he to them. This means you do not have to carry that isolation as a final separation. You can notice the familiar presence in the people and moments around you today, letting that steadiness be enough.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna has asked how a person can keep a steady mind while living in the world. Krishna replies that the one who sees him in every being and sees every being within him will never be separated from him, nor he from that person. You do not have to carry this loneliness as a final wall. The presence you are missing can show up in the ordinary people and moments around you today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You feel lonely while studying. Krishna tells Arjuna, See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me. This means that noticing connection in ordinary moments and in the world around you can mean you are never fully out of sight. When you sit with your books today, look for one small thing around you that feels part of a larger whole, and let that be a quiet reminder that you are not out of reach.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching him how to meditate and what a settled mind looks like. Arjuna has been asking about the nature of the yogi and the path of meditation. Krishna tells him that whoever sees him everywhere and sees everything resting in him will never be lost to him, and he will never be lost to that person. You are studying far from home and the quiet feels heavy. This verse says that noticing a thread of connection in ordinary moments can remind you that you are still within reach.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You carry a peaceful feeling even while working. Krishna tells Arjuna that the one whose happiness, delight, and light are all within becomes one with Brahman and reaches its peace. That inner glow can be your own steady ground today, a quiet source you return to amid the day.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He describes the person who has seen clearly. This person finds happiness inside, delight inside, and light inside. Such a yogi joins with Brahman and reaches its peace while still living. The verse says pleasures that begin and end cannot hold your happiness. You could find your joy from within. You already feel peaceful inside your work. That quiet steadiness can be your own ground today, a source you return to amid the day.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: You feel inspired as you run your own thing. Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is the one the world follows. As someone building something of your own, your daily choices quietly shape how those around you work and respond. Let the way you handle success today be the standard you naturally leave behind.
meaning: Krishna speaks this to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just urged Arjuna to act for the good of the world. Now he explains that people do not learn from words alone. They watch those they respect and copy their actions. Even a fulfilled person keeps working because the world looks to them for the standard to follow. Your inspiration carries weight now that you run your own thing. The way you move through success today quietly teaches those around you what is possible.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is the one people follow. As you study and feel inspired, your actions quietly shape how those around you learn to work and handle pressure. Let your own effort set the tone you would want them to see.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You feel grateful right now. The poet says he does not know what generous austerity ripened into this freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, good company, and a mind that stirs only gently. You might rest in wondering at the calm and dignity already present in your working days, rather than taking them for granted.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines from his Worship of Shiva. He is reflecting on the life of a quiet seeker by the Ganga. He lists freedom to move, food taken with dignity, noble company, and study that ends in calm. He wonders aloud what generous austerity in past days could have ripened into such a plain and self-respecting life. He treats these ordinary goods as a rare blessing rather than a given. You are working through your days with a sense of gratitude. The poet invites you to notice the dignity and calm already woven into your ordinary routine.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You carry a hopeful feeling as you step into this new beginning. Lakshmana tells Ram that there is no strength greater than enthusiasm, and for the one who has it, nothing is out of reach. That energy of will can meet you right where you are, perhaps in a small morning walk or a single new routine you choose to begin.
meaning: At Lake Pampa in spring, Rama sits overwhelmed by grief after Sita has been taken. Every living thing around him reminds him of her, and his sorrow deepens. Lakshman, his younger brother, speaks to him and says that enthusiasm is powerful. There is no strength greater than this enthusiasm. For the person who holds it, nothing in the world is out of reach. You are beginning something new with hope already in your chest. That same energy of will can carry you forward from where you stand now.

verse_text.speaker: Savitri
verse_text.setting: Knowing her husband will die in three days, Savitri takes a hard three-night vow; her father-in-law worries.
verse_text.line: I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end.
verse_text.translation: Don't be distressed, father. I will see this vow through. It was begun with determination, and determination is what carries it to the end.

reading: You feel determined to keep a resolve. Savitri tells her father-in-law that she began her hard vow with determination, and that same determination will carry it to the end. Let that steady resolve be what moves you forward now, step by step, until the resolve itself reaches its close.
meaning: Savitri speaks to her blind father-in-law Dyumatsena. She knows her husband Satyavan will die in three days. She has begun a severe three-night vow without food. Dyumatsena is distressed by its harshness. Savitri tells him she started this with determination, and that same determination will carry it to the end. Steady love and clear speech can face even death. Determination carries what fear would drop. You began this resolve with clear intent. Let that same steady force move you forward now, step by step, until the work itself reaches its close.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You feel curious, and Krishna tells Arjuna that people turn to the divine in many ways—distress, curiosity, need, or wisdom. All four kinds are counted among the good. Your curiosity today is one of those welcome doors, a sign that you are already walking toward what matters.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He says all four kinds worship him. In plain modern words, whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. Your curiosity is one of those four doors. It places you among those who are already walking toward what matters.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You are curious right now, and Krishna says that those who seek knowledge are among the good who turn to the divine. Your curiosity itself is a welcome door. It places you among those who are counted as noble simply for wanting to understand.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just explained that deluded people do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He says all four kinds worship him. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. Distress, curiosity, need, and wisdom are all valid doors. Your curiosity about this text places you among those who are counted as good simply for wanting to understand. It is a valid door into the search, not a lesser one.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You feel anxious while raising your kids. Krishna tells Arjuna that contact between the senses and their objects brings heat and cold, pleasure and pain, and these come and go without lasting. You might notice this discomfort, like shifting weather, also has a beginning and an end. You can bear it patiently without letting panic take over.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that the true self never dies and never is born. Yet the body feels heat and cold, pleasure and pain when the senses meet the world. These feelings come and go. They do not last. So Arjuna must bear them with patience. The self outlasts every passing ache and loss. Your anxiety while raising your children is a passing contact between your senses and a hard moment. It has a beginning and an end, and it does not last forever.

verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.

meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that the senses meeting their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These feelings come and go and do not last. He asks Arjuna to bear them patiently. Your anxious moments while caring for your parents also arrive and depart. They do not last forever.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You feel anxious as you move through this season of life. Krishna tells Arjuna that contact between the senses and the world brings heat and cold, pleasure and pain, and these states come and go without lasting. You might notice this anxious wave as something that arrives and departs, without letting it carry you away.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield after Arjuna has laid down his weapons in grief. Arjuna fears that if the self is eternal, then all this suffering is pointless. Krishna answers that the true self is never born and never dies, but the body is subject to contact between the senses and the world. From that contact come heat and cold, pleasure and pain. These states arise and pass away by nature. They do not last. Therefore one must bear them without being carried away by either joy or grief. Your anxiety now is a state that arises from contact and will pass, without defining the self that remains beneath it.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: You feel restless while running your own thing. Bali says, 'Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.' That same loop can wear on you today. You might notice the days blurring into one another without a clear sense of where they lead. Let that recognition sit with you, and look for one small teaching or shift that changes the shape of your next task.
meaning: Bali, the demon king who has ruled the three worlds for ages, sits by his window and looks out at his life. He has done the same things day after day, night after night, and he asks what any of it adds up to. He remembers a riddle his father Virochana once told him. The riddle speaks of a vast realm ruled by a silent king and an all-powerful minister. The minister is the mind. Bali realizes that winning the mind over, through practice, is what wins everything. You are running your own work and the same tasks keep returning. That loop can feel like a mockery to a thoughtful mind.

verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

reading: You feel uneasy, as if you are not good enough. Manu speaks of standing before the wishing tree yet hesitating to ask for what he truly wants, not knowing its power. That doubt in your heart today might be hiding a wish you are afraid to name; the tree is there regardless, and your asking does not depend on how small you feel.
meaning: King Manu and Queen Shatarupa have spent years in the forest doing austerity. Lord Vishnu appears and tells them to ask for any boon. Manu feels his own smallness. He compares himself to a poor man who finds a wishing tree yet still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing how generous the tree is. He holds back because he doubts his worthiness, even though the power to fulfill his wish is right there. That unease you carry might be hiding a wish you have not yet dared to name. The verse suggests the hesitation comes from feeling too small, not from any lack in what is offered.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You carry the weight of overthinking while raising your kids. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, as hard to hold as the wind. This verse names that struggle plainly, showing that a mind that will not settle is not a personal failure. When the thoughts race, you can rest in the honest admission that holding them is difficult, just as Arjuna did.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He has just heard that a steady mind sees all beings' joy and pain as his own. He objects that such evenness cannot last. The mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and he thinks it is as hard to hold as the wind. The verse proposes that the mind is difficult to steady, yet practice and letting go can train it.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You feel empty. Young Rama asks what kingship or pleasure means to him, and who he is and what it is all for. When nothing feels like it matters, that question can be a doorway rather than an end. Let the unreality of it be unreal, and rest with who you are right now.
meaning: Young Rama has returned from his travels and sits in his father's court. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask why he seems so low. Rama answers by questioning everything around him. He asks what kingship or pleasure mean to him, and who he is and what it is all for. He says if the world is unreal, let it be unreal. The text treats this honest questioning as the healthy start of inquiry, not as despair to be fixed. You have stepped back from work and the days feel hollow. Rama names that same emptiness without rushing to fix it, and invites you to rest with the question of who you are now.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You are feeling angry while raising your kids. Krishna tells Arjuna that when someone dwells on objects, attachment is born, and from that attachment comes desire, which blocked turns into anger. This verse speaks to your today by showing that anger can grow from dwelling on what you want. You might notice where your mind keeps returning as you go about the day.
meaning: Krishna answers Arjuna after Arjuna asks what a person of steady wisdom looks like in speech, sitting and walking. Krishna traces how the mind moves. When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire, and when desire is blocked, anger arises. The verse proposes that steadiness is built by guarding where attention rests, because anger starts with what a person keeps dwelling on. Your anger while raising your kids may have started long before the flare, in something your mind kept returning to. The verse shows that the dwelling stage is where the shift happens, and that is where your attention lives today.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You feel empty right now. The text records that Rama no longer lights up at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work; he simply keeps silent. That quiet withdrawal can be a real state worth noticing, and letting someone bring you help is okay.
meaning: A servant tells King Dasharatha that his son Rama has come home from a long pilgrimage and now shows no interest in anything. He does not laugh at jokes, he does not enjoy pleasures, and he does not stay with his work. He simply sits in silence. The text presents this quiet withdrawal as a serious state that calls for care and conversation rather than scolding.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You feel anxious right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that contact between the senses and objects brings heat and cold, pleasure and pain, and these come and go without lasting. You can notice this discomfort as something with a beginning and an end, bearing it without letting panic take over. When the next wave of unease arrives, simply observe that it, too, will pass.

Krishna tells him that the self within never comes into being and never perishes. Sense contact with objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These arrive and depart like shifts in the air. They do not endure. Therefore Arjuna must bear them without surrendering to either joy or sorrow. Your anxiety rises from sense contact with the pressures around you. It is a passing state, not the whole of who you are, and it will move on.

verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people turn to the divine: those in distress, those seeking wealth, those seeking knowledge, and the wise. Your curiosity places you among those welcome at this door. You may simply sit with that question today, letting it be enough that you are here.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. It does not require a pure motive or a settled mind. Your curiosity is one of the four doors that leads here. It places you among those who are already counted as good.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

meaning: Bali speaks these words to himself while sitting alone by his window. He has ruled the three worlds for ages. He sees the same days and nights return, the same chain of tasks. He feels mocked by the repetition. The verse proposes that when life feels like a loop, the work is not more of it but mastering the mind that runs it. Your restlessness is not a sign that your work is worthless. It is the first honest signal that your mind is still awake enough to ask what the loop is for.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You carry a peaceful feeling even while working. Krishna tells Arjuna that the one whose happiness, delight, and light are all within finds lasting freedom. That inner steadiness can meet you today, as you move through your day, simply as the quiet glow already present inside you.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield while teaching the yoga of knowledge. He describes the wise person who sees clearly. This person keeps happiness, delight and light inside. Such a yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman. The verse says pleasures that start and end cannot hold your happiness. You could find the joy within. That quiet glow you carry while working is already the inner steadiness this verse points to. It is not waiting somewhere else.

verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?

You might let yourself wonder at these ordinary dignities you already hold, rather than taking them for granted.

He has just reflected that moonlight, poetry and good company lose their charm once the mind sees how fleeting they are, and that the wise leave palaces for the forest. Here he lists the goods of the renunciant's life. He wonders what generous austerity ripened into this plain existence.

verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people worship him: those in distress, those seeking knowledge, those in need, and the wise. Your curiosity places you among those welcomed without condition. Let this truth sit with you as you care for your parents today.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He says all four kinds worship him. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. Distress, curiosity, need, or wisdom are all valid doors. Your curiosity about these words places you among those who are welcomed without condition as you tend to your parents.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You are feeling angry right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that when someone dwells on objects, attachment is born, and from that attachment comes desire, which blocked turns into anger. This verse suggests your anger may have started earlier, in the mind dwelling on what it wanted. You might notice where your attention has been resting today, and what it has been turning toward.
meaning: Krishna answers Arjuna, who has asked what a person of steady mind looks like. Krishna explains that when a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire, and when that desire is blocked, it turns into anger. Steadiness comes from guarding where the mind rests. Your anger may have begun earlier than the moment it showed, in the part of your mind that kept returning to what it wanted.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that people turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom, and all four are welcome. You are arriving with curiosity, and that door is already open. The verse counts your wondering as a way in, not a halfway step.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He says all four worship him. The point is that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. Your curiosity is not a half step. It is one of the four doors the verse already counts as good.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You feel anxious right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that contact between the senses and their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and these pass. You can notice this discomfort as something that begins and ends, without letting panic sweep you away. Let this feeling be like the weather Krishna describes, rising and falling on its own.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that the true self is never born and never dies. Yet the body still meets the world. Contact between the senses and their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These feelings come and go. They do not last. Arjuna must bear them patiently. What you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain. You are anxious right now. This verse suggests that your anxiety, like the weather Krishna describes, has a beginning and an end. It does not define what you truly are underneath it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Without inner discipline there's no clarity; without clarity, no peace; and without peace, where is happiness?
verse_text.translation: For the undisciplined there is no understanding and no steady contemplation. Without contemplation there is no peace, and for the one without peace, where is happiness?

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that without inner discipline there is no clarity, and without clarity there is no peace, so without peace, where is happiness? The verse sees stress stealing happiness as a chain reaction: an unsettled mind loses its focus, and then peace slips away. Amid the pressure of booking your tatkal ticket, this points to the mind needing a place to stand before relief can settle.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on working in the world without being stained by it.
verse_text.line: Like a lotus leaf in water, do your work without letting the mess soak in.
verse_text.translation: One who acts offering all actions to the Supreme, giving up attachment, is not touched by wrong, as a lotus leaf is not wet by water.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to work like a lotus leaf in water, letting the mess roll off without soaking in. You carry the pressure of constant deadlines and demands. You can do your work fully while keeping your inner surface dry, letting the surrounding chaos bead and fall away.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Rivers pour into the ocean and it stays full and still. Let desires enter you the same way.
verse_text.translation: As waters enter the ocean, which is ever being filled yet stays unmoved within its shores, so the one into whom all desires enter in the same way finds peace, not the one who craves desires.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that rivers pour into the ocean yet it stays full and still. Demands will keep coming, but peace belongs to the one who takes them in without being moved. This steadiness gives you ground to stand on amid the pressure of your booking timing, without asking you to absorb everything.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Moderate in food and rest, in work and play, in sleep and waking: that's how sorrow eases.
verse_text.translation: For one who is moderate in food and recreation, measured in effort at work, moderate in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that yoga ends sorrow when food, rest, work and sleep are kept in measure. You could try setting one fixed boundary today, such as a hard stop for work or a set bedtime, so your body gets a rhythm amid the pressure. This steadiness supports the calm you are building through the week.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on acting free of ego, like and dislike, in your own way.
verse_text.line: Hand your work to something higher, drop the 'mine' and the hoping, and act with the fever gone.
verse_text.translation: Surrendering all actions to me, with your mind on the inner self, free from hope and the sense of 'mine', fight with your fever gone.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to hand his work over to something higher, drop the sense of 'mine', and act with the fever gone. You could try this before your next booking task: consciously offer the action to something larger than your worry, then do it without the anxious grip. Let the work move through you while your mind rests on what is steady.

story.title: Janaka on the palace roof
story.summary: Walking in his garden one spring, King Janaka overheard hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbed to his palace roof and questioned everything he had lived for. When his attendant came to call him to the day's work, he could have walked away from the throne. He didn't. He went back and did his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutched.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

days.reading: King Janaka heard sages sing of the self, climbed to his palace roof, and questioned everything. When his attendant called him to duty, he could have walked away from the throne, but he returned and did his work with a mind that no longer clutched. This speaks to your anxious pressure around tatkal ticket booking timing: you can face the rush without letting it grip you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of people turn to the divine: those in distress, those seeking knowledge, those in need, and the wise. Your curiosity places you among those welcomed. The verse simply counts you as one of the good, without asking what comes next.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He says all four worship him. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. Distress, curiosity, need, and wisdom are all valid doors. Your curiosity counts. The verse places you among those who are already welcome, without asking what comes next.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You feel hopeful about what lies ahead. Lakshmana tells Ram that enthusiasm is powerful, and for the one who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach. That energy of will can be the first step you take toward a new beginning, even before the path ahead is clear.
meaning: At Lake Pampa in spring, Rama is overwhelmed by longing for Sita. Every bird and mated deer reminds him of her, and his grief deepens. Lakshmana answers this lament by telling him that enthusiasm is powerful. There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach. You feel hopeful about what lies ahead. That same energy of will can be the first step you take toward a new beginning, even before the path ahead is clear.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You feel lost right now. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed by grief to go on. This verse names the moment of setting everything down when you simply cannot carry on. The story does not end there; the very next verses move toward asking for help and finding a way forward.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra from the battlefield. He reports that Arjuna has dropped his bow and arrows and sat down in his chariot. His mind is overcome by grief. The verse presents this collapse as the true starting point of the teaching. It shows that even the strongest people can freeze when sorrow hits.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You carry a peaceful feeling even while working. Krishna says the one whose happiness, delight and light are all within becomes one with Brahman and reaches its peace. That inner gladness can stay steady for you today, not because the outside is perfect, but because your own light is already lit.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He is describing the wise person who sees clearly. This person keeps their happiness, delight and light inside. They do not depend on things that come and go. Because their joy comes from within, they reach lasting freedom while still alive. You already feel peaceful inside your work. That calm can stay with you today because it comes from your own steadiness, not from how the shift goes.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that people turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom, and all four are welcome. Your curiosity places you among those good people who seek the divine. You can rest in that door today, simply as it is.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. These are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He says all four worship him. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. Your curiosity is already a valid way in. It places you among those who turn toward something larger, without any proof of past worth required.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: You feel restless right now. The Yoga Vasishtha has Bali say that day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over, and to a thinking person this feels like a mockery. That sense of endless repetition can sit with you today without deciding what your studying means. Let the loop simply be there, as Bali noticed it by his window.
meaning: The demon king Bali has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day he sits by his window and notices that day follows night and the same tasks return without end. He speaks these words to himself. He says that to a thinking person this endless chain feels like a mockery. The verse proposes that when life feels like a loop, the work is not to add more of it but to master the mind that runs it. Your studying can feel like that same chain right now, and the verse names the weariness without calling it failure.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: You feel inspired right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is the one the world follows. As you raise your kids, your daily choices quietly shape how they learn to work and handle pressure. Let your grounded effort be the example they naturally take up.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after urging him to act for the good of the world. He explains that people do not simply follow words. They watch what someone respected actually does. Whatever standard that person lives by, others copy it. The verse proposes that even those who have no personal need to act must keep working, because the world looks to them and follows their lead. You are raising children while feeling inspired. Your daily conduct quietly teaches them more than any instruction. The standard you set through your own grounded effort becomes the one they naturally take up.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people turn to the divine: those in distress, those seeking wealth, those seeking knowledge, and the wise. You are standing at the door of curiosity, and that path is named among the welcomed. Let this verse sit with you as a quiet confirmation that your wondering is already a kind of arrival.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, the seeker of wealth, the seeker of knowledge, and the wise. He says all four worship him. In plain modern words, people come to the divine through trouble, through wanting something, through wondering about truth, or through steady wisdom. The verse proposes that none of these doors is closed.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

days.reading: Arjuna tells Krishna his mind is confused about what is right and asks him to teach him plainly what is best. Like you, drawn to Rishikesh by curiosity, he stands between two choices that both feel wrong and admits he cannot see the way forward alone. He offers himself as a student ready to learn, not to surrender his conscience, but to receive clarity before acting.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that contact between the senses and objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain, which come and go and do not last. You can let this stressful stretch be like weather that shifts on its own. Notice the discomfort without letting it sweep you away, and keep your feet on the ground right where you are.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse_text.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits, and not to cling to inaction. This speaks to a curiosity that is quietly weighing outcomes against effort. You can give your full attention to the craft and showing up, letting the result be what it will be, without letting the outcome own you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse_text.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to lift himself by his own effort and not let himself sink, since the self alone is the friend of the self and the enemy of the self. You could notice the next harsh thought about your search and gently turn it into one kind, steady step. This keeps you from sinking while you keep looking.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.
verse_text.line: Learn from those who have seen the truth: approach with humility, ask real questions, and serve.
verse_text.translation: Learn it by bowing down, by questioning, and by service. Those who are wise and have seen the truth will teach you that knowledge.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to learn from those who have seen the truth by approaching with humility, asking real questions, and serving. Since you are curious about where to start with the Gita, you could seek one trustworthy commentary or study circle today and bring a humble question to it. Ask what the text actually says rather than what you assume, and offer your attention as your form of service.

story.title: Action with devotion: surrender
story.summary: Krishna urges Arjuna to offer all action, warns that ego will only trip him, tells him to reflect fully and then choose, and finally to take refuge in him alone and not grieve.
story.lesson: Reflect fully, choose freely, and set down the fear.

days.reading: After eighteen chapters to a student who once refused, the Lord says he has shared the most secret knowledge and asks him to reflect fully and then do as he wishes. Because you are dear to the teacher, the final word is refuge alone and the command not to grieve. Your curiosity can rest in that open choice and the concrete promise to be freed from all wrongs.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You are studying and feel curious. Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people worship him: those in distress, those seeking knowledge, those in need, and the wise. Your curiosity places you among those welcome to turn toward the divine. Let this open door meet you exactly where you are today.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after explaining that deluded people do not turn to him. He names four kinds of good people who do turn. These are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He says all four worship him. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. It does not require a pure motive or a settled mind. Your curiosity right now is one of those doors. It places you among those who are welcome to turn toward the divine, without needing another reason first.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people turn to the divine: those in distress, those seeking knowledge, those in need, and the wise. Your curiosity places you among those welcome seekers. Let this openness meet the quiet days ahead.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded do not seek him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He says all four worship him. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. Distress, curiosity, need, and wisdom are all valid doors. Your curiosity about these words already places you among those who are welcome here. It does not need to hide behind pain or duty to count as real.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of people turn to the divine: those in distress, those seeking wealth, those seeking knowledge, and the wise. Your curiosity places you among those welcome to approach. It is enough that you are drawn to learn right now.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that deluded people do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, the seeker of wealth, the seeker of knowledge, and the wise. He says all four worship him. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. Distress, curiosity, need, and wisdom are all valid doors. You are running your own thing right now. Your curiosity about the Gita is one of those four doors. It is enough that you want to learn.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: My heart feels heavy as stone, but I don't cry, because of what people would think.
verse_text.translation: Though my heart is packed tight with the stones of life's sorrows, I don't let my tears fall, only out of fear of what my own people would think.

reading: It sounds like you're carrying something very heavy right now.

verse_text.line: My heart feels heavy as stone, but I don't cry, because of what people would think.
verse_text.translation: Though my heart is packed tight with the stones of life's sorrows, I don't let my tears fall, only out of fear of what my own people would think.

verse_text.speaker: Angiras
verse_text.setting: The two birds, continued.
verse_text.line: The bird that eats grieves, lost in its helplessness. When it sees the calm one beside it, grief falls away.
verse_text.translation: On the same tree a person sits sunk, grieving, bewildered by his own helplessness. When he sees the other, the content lord, and his greatness, his sorrow leaves him.

verse_text.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles – First Series, CIII, p. 160
verse_text.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse_text.setting: Letter from Belur, 18 May 1901, ill and grieving the sudden death of the Raja of Khetri.
verse_text.line: Yet I am sure to bob up soon and am waiting for the next turn.
verse_text.translation: The Raja of Khetri died from a fall a few months ago. So you see things are all gloomy with me just now, and my own health is wretched. Yet I am sure to bob up soon and am waiting for the next turn.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: Closing verse of the section on steadfastness.
verse_text.line: A cut tree grows back; the waning moon fills again. Remembering this, the wise do not despair.
verse_text.translation: A tree that is cut grows again; the waning moon waxes again in the world. Reflecting on this, the good are not tormented in this world.

verse_text.speaker: Vasishtha
verse_text.setting: Vasishtha on the fourth gatekeeper: good company (satsanga).
verse_text.line: Even at your lowest and most helpless, don't let go of good company.
verse_text.translation: Even when people fall into the hardest straits and feel helpless, they should not let go of good company, not even a little.

verse_text.speaker: Kabandha
verse_text.setting: Ram is lost and grieving; Kabandha tells him to seek Sugriva, who has also lost his wife and home.
verse_text.line: Find a friend who knows your kind of trouble. You won't get through this alone.
verse_text.translation: You must make him your friend, best of friends. Thinking it over, I see no success for you without it.

story.title: Kabandha: find a friend who understands
story.summary: Freed from a curse, the creature Kabandha tells the grieving brothers to seek out Sugriva, an exile who has also lost his wife and home. Only a friend in the same trouble, he says, can help them now.
story.lesson: When you are lost, look for someone who has been through the same thing.

verse_text.speaker: Vidura
verse_text.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
verse_text.line: If you fear someone's anger or must tiptoe around them, they are not really your friend.
verse_text.translation: That is no friend whose anger you fear, or whom you must approach warily. A friend is one you can trust as you trust a father; the rest are mere acquaintances.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram, having embraced Vibhishan, asks how he survived in Lanka.
verse_text.line: You lived among the cruel day and night. I know how you kept your goodness.
verse_text.translation: 'You lived day and night among the wicked; how did you keep your goodness, friend? I know all your ways: very wise in conduct, with no taste for wrong.'

verse_text.speaker: Seer
verse_text.setting: The creation story: last of all, dharma is made.
verse_text.line: Nothing is higher than what is right. With it the weak can face the strong. What is right is truth.
verse_text.translation: Still he did not flourish. So he created a higher form, dharma. Dharma is the power over power; nothing is higher than dharma. Through dharma even a weak man can stand up to a strong one, as with the help of a king. That dharma is truth. So people say of one who speaks truth, 'He speaks dharma,' and of one who speaks dharma, 'He speaks truth.' Both are the same.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked.
verse_text.line: Avoid a cruel person even if brilliant. A snake wearing a jewel still bites.
verse_text.translation: A wicked person should be avoided, even if adorned with learning. Is a snake any less frightening because it wears a jewel?

story.title: Shunahshepa, the son neither parent chose to keep
story.summary: A king needs a human substitute for a lost sacrifice and offers a fortune for a son. The father says: I will never sell my eldest. The mother says: the youngest is my darling, I cannot part with him. The middle boy hears both sentences and understands his place in the house. He says it himself: then the middle one is sold. Take me.
story.lesson: When those who should protect you do not, you may seek refuge elsewhere and ask plainly for what you need.
